s3-micro-01.stem: A university agricultural research station has 120 researcher-hours available this season. The table shows the researcher-hours each of four requested field projects would require. Which of the following statements best describes how the table illustrates the economic concept of scarcity?

stimulus.description: Table of four field projects a research station wants to run this season, with the researcher-hours each requires. The station has 120 researcher-hours available.

data.title: Field projects requested at a university agricultural research station

options.text: The projects together require more researcher-hours than are available, so running some projects means giving up others.
options.why: Key: total requested hours (155) exceed the 120 available, so wants exceed resources and choosing requires trade-offs.

options.text: The station has too few researcher-hours to complete even one of the four projects, so no project can be run.
options.why: Misconception: confuses scarcity with absolute lack of resources; each project needs 50 or fewer hours, so several can be run.

options.text: The irrigation trial requires the most hours, so it is the project that must be given up first.
options.why: Misconception: believes scarcity dictates which good is dropped based on resource use alone, ignoring opportunity cost and the value of each project.

options.text: Scarcity arises because the station could get more researcher-hours if it paid higher wages, so hours are not truly limited.
options.why: Misconception: thinks scarcity vanishes if more resources can be obtained at some price; scarcity is about limited resources relative to wants, even when purchasable.

options.text: Researcher-hours are scarce only if every project is run, so scarcity would disappear once any two projects are chosen.
options.why: Misconception: thinks scarcity depends on the particular choice made; in fact the resource is limited relative to wants regardless, and any choice still forgoes the other projects.

s3-micro-01.explanation_en: The projects require 40 + 35 + 50 + 30 = 155 researcher-hours, but only 120 are available. Wants exceed available resources, which is scarcity, so choosing some projects means forgoing others. The statement that no project can be run is wrong because each project needs fewer than 120 hours; scarcity does not mean having nothing. The statement that the irrigation trial must be dropped first is wrong because scarcity does not determine which project is dropped; that depends on the value of the alternatives forgone. The statement that hours are not truly limited if more could be bought is wrong because a resource is scarce whenever it is limited relative to wants, even if it can be obtained at a cost. The statement that scarcity disappears once two projects are chosen is wrong because the limit on hours persists and the unchosen projects are still forgone.

s3-micro-02.stem: The clinic's director observes that the 180 weekly hours requested exceed the 120 hours available, so the director must decide how to allocate the hours. Which of the following best explains why this situation illustrates scarcity?

stimulus.description: Table of weekly requests for physical therapist (PT) hours at a university sports-medicine clinic, compared with the PT hours available.

data.title: Weekly PT hours at a university sports-medicine clinic
data.note: The clinic cannot hire additional therapists this year.

options.text: The available PT hours are limited relative to the wants for them, so using hours for one purpose means giving up other uses.
options.why: Correct: scarcity is limited resources versus unlimited wants, forcing choices and opportunity costs.

options.text: The clinic charges students too little for walk-in treatment, so the director must raise prices until requests equal 120 hours.
options.why: Misconception: scarcity is a pricing problem that exists only when price is too low; scarcity exists at any price.

options.text: The clinic is operating inefficiently, so scarcity would disappear if the director used the 120 hours more productively.
options.why: Misconception: scarcity results from inefficiency; even fully efficient use leaves wants exceeding resources.

options.text: Scarcity exists only because the clinic is a nonprofit, so a for-profit clinic would have enough PT hours for all requests.
options.why: Misconception: scarcity depends on organization type or profit motive; it affects all economies and organizations.

options.text: The requests total 180 hours, so the clinic has a shortage that would not exist if the clinic hired additional therapists.
options.why: Misconception: scarcity equals a temporary shortage that more hiring would eliminate; extra therapists are themselves scarce and wants remain unlimited.

s3-micro-02.explanation_en: Scarcity means resources are limited while wants are effectively unlimited, so choices are required and every use of PT hours has an opportunity cost. The first option states this. The pricing option confuses scarcity with a price-setting problem; scarcity exists at any price. The inefficiency option is wrong because even perfectly efficient use cannot make 120 hours satisfy 180 hours of requests. The nonprofit option is wrong because scarcity affects every organization and economy, for-profit or not. The hiring option confuses scarcity with a temporary shortage; additional therapists would use scarce resources and wants would still exceed what is available.

s3-micro-03.stem: A family farm can produce corn and soybeans with a fixed amount of land and equipment. Its production possibilities are shown in the table. As the farm moves from point A to point E, each additional 10 tons of corn costs more soybeans than the previous 10 tons. Which of the following best explains why this occurs?

stimulus.description: Table of five efficient production combinations of corn and soybeans for a family farm in one season, using all its land and equipment.

data.title: Family farm production possibilities (tons per season)
data.note: All points are efficient; the farm uses all of its land and equipment at each point.

options.text: The farm's total resources shrink as it grows more corn, so fewer soybeans can be grown at each point.
options.why: Confuses movement along the PPC with a shrinking resource base; resources are fixed and fully used at every point.

options.text: Technology for growing corn improves with each additional ton produced, which lowers the soybean output given up.
options.why: Confuses movement along the PPC with a technology change; technology would shift the curve outward, and it would not raise opportunity cost.

options.text: Land is not equally productive in both crops, so the land moved to corn later is increasingly better suited to soybeans.
options.why: Correct: resources are specialized, so shifting them to corn means moving land with comparative advantage in soybeans, giving rising opportunity cost.

options.text: The price of corn rises as the farm grows more of it, which raises the soybeans given up for each ton.
options.why: Introduces prices, which are not part of the PPC; opportunity cost here is measured in physical output given up, not in dollar prices.

options.text: The farm is producing inefficiently at the points between A and E, so extra corn requires giving up more soybeans.
options.why: Misreads efficient points as inefficient; the table states all points are efficient and inefficiency would not explain increasing opportunity cost.

s3-micro-03.explanation_en: Opportunity cost of corn per ton is 4/10 = 0.4, 6/10 = 0.6, 10/10 = 1.0, then 20/10 = 2.0 soybeans, so it rises. This happens because resources are not equally suited to both goods: the farm first uses land best for corn, and as it expands corn it must move land that is much better at soybeans, so more soybeans are lost per ton of corn. Better corn technology is wrong because technology shifts the whole curve and would not raise the cost along it. Shrinking resources is wrong because land and equipment are fixed and fully used. Rising corn prices is wrong because the PPC measures opportunity cost in output, not dollars. Inefficiency is wrong because every point shown is efficient.

s3-micro-04.stem: A sports medicine clinic uses all of its staff and equipment efficiently to produce fitness assessments and therapy sessions. The table shows the combinations it can produce each week. As the clinic moves from combination A to B to C to D to E, the number of therapy sessions given up for each additional 10 assessments rises. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

stimulus.description: Weekly production possibilities of a sports medicine clinic using all staff and equipment efficiently.

options.text: The clinic is operating inside its production possibilities curve, so some resources are idle and must be reallocated at higher cost.
options.why: Misconception: confuses efficient points on the curve with inefficiency inside it; the stem says resources are used efficiently.

options.text: Staff and equipment are not equally well suited to both activities, so resources moved into assessments become progressively less productive there.
options.why: Correct: specialized resources yield increasing opportunity cost, a bowed-out PPC.

options.text: Technological improvement in therapy has shifted the production possibilities curve outward, raising the cost of assessments.
options.why: Misconception: confuses a shift of the PPC with movement along it; no change in technology occurs.

options.text: Resources are perfectly adaptable between the two activities, so each extra assessment costs the same number of therapy sessions.
options.why: Misconception: describes constant opportunity cost (straight-line PPC), which contradicts the table's rising cost.

options.text: Demand for fitness assessments is rising, which raises the price and therefore the opportunity cost of producing them.
options.why: Misconception: attributes opportunity cost to demand and price rather than resource productivity trade-offs.

s3-micro-04.explanation_en: Giving up 4, 8, 12, then 20 therapy sessions for each additional 10 assessments shows increasing opportunity cost. This occurs because resources are not equally suited to both uses: the first resources moved are best at assessments, and later ones are better at therapy, so more therapy is lost per assessment gained. The idle-resources explanation is wrong because all points are efficient and lie on the curve. The technology explanation is wrong because that would shift the curve, while this is movement along it. The perfectly adaptable resources explanation would give a constant cost, which the table contradicts. The rising demand explanation is wrong because the PPC reflects production trade-offs, not prices or demand.

s3-micro-05.stem: Two agricultural field stations, Alder and Birch, can each grow wheat and soybeans. The table shows the maximum daily output of each crop if a station devotes all of its plots to that crop. Opportunity costs are constant. Which of the following correctly identifies the comparative advantage based on the data?

stimulus.description: Table of maximum daily output for two agricultural research stations if each devotes all its plots to a single crop.

data.title: Maximum daily output if all plots are devoted to one crop
data.note: Each station's opportunity cost is constant (linear production possibilities).

options.text: Alder has the comparative advantage in soybeans, because it gives up 3 bushels of wheat per bushel of soybeans while Birch gives up 9.
options.why: Correct: opportunity cost of a soybean is 60/20 = 3 wheat for Alder and 45/5 = 9 wheat for Birch; the lower cost means Alder's comparative advantage is soybeans.

options.text: Alder has the comparative advantage in both crops, because it can produce more of each crop per day than Birch.
options.why: Confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage; one station cannot have the lower opportunity cost in both goods.

options.text: Birch has the comparative advantage in soybeans, because it gives up only 1/9 bushel of soybeans per bushel of wheat.
options.why: Misreads the ratio: 1/9 soybean is Birch's cost of producing wheat, which indicates Birch's advantage in wheat, not soybeans.

options.text: Alder has the comparative advantage in wheat, because it can produce 60 bushels of wheat, more than Birch's 45.
options.why: Uses larger output (absolute advantage) as the criterion; Alder's opportunity cost of wheat (1/3 soybean) is higher than Birch's (1/9).

options.text: Neither station has a comparative advantage, because Alder is more productive than Birch in both crops.
options.why: Believes that absolute advantage in both goods eliminates comparative advantage; opportunity costs still differ, so each station has one.

s3-micro-05.explanation_en: Compute opportunity costs. Alder gives up 60/20 = 3 bushels of wheat per bushel of soybeans; Birch gives up 45/5 = 9 bushels of wheat. Alder's lower cost gives it the comparative advantage in soybeans (and Birch has it in wheat: 1/9 versus 1/3 soybean per wheat). The claim that Alder has the advantage in both crops is wrong because it confuses absolute with comparative advantage, and comparative advantage cannot belong to one party in both goods. The claim that Birch has the advantage in soybeans misattributes the 1/9 figure, which is Birch's cost of wheat. The claim that Alder has the advantage in wheat uses raw output, but Alder's wheat cost of 1/3 soybean exceeds Birch's 1/9. The claim that there is no comparative advantage is wrong because opportunity costs differ, so each station has a comparative advantage in one good.

s3-micro-06.stem: Dana and Eli share a kitchen and each can spend an hour making only loaves of bread, only jars of jam, or a combination at a constant trade-off, as shown in the table. Based on the data, which statement correctly identifies how they should specialize and why?

stimulus.description: Hourly output of two roommates, each spending one hour on either bread or jam.

data.title: Maximum output in one hour (using all hour on one good)
data.units: output per hour, constant opportunity cost

options.text: Dana should specialize in bread and Eli in jam, because Dana produces more loaves per hour than Eli does.
options.why: Compares raw output rather than opportunity cost; Dana's higher bread output does not imply a lower opportunity cost.

options.text: Dana should specialize in both goods and Eli in neither, because Dana can produce more of each good per hour.
options.why: Confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage; ignores that one person cannot have a comparative advantage in both goods.

options.text: Dana should specialize in jam and Eli in bread, because Eli gives up 1 jar per loaf while Dana gives up 2 jars per loaf.
options.why: Correct: Eli's opportunity cost of bread (1 jar) is below Dana's (2 jars), so Eli has the comparative advantage in bread and Dana in jam (0.5 loaf vs 1 loaf).

options.text: Dana should specialize in bread and Eli in jam, because Eli gives up 1 loaf per jar while Dana gives up 2 loaves per jar.
options.why: Inverts the opportunity costs: Dana gives up 0.5 loaf per jar and Eli gives up 1 loaf per jar, so Dana, not Eli, has the lower cost of jam.

options.text: Dana and Eli cannot gain from specializing, because Dana has an absolute advantage in producing both goods.
options.why: Believes trade requires that one party be better at nothing; gains from trade depend on differing opportunity costs, not absolute advantage.

s3-micro-06.explanation_en: Opportunity cost of one loaf: Dana gives up 12/6 = 2 jars, Eli gives up 4/4 = 1 jar. Eli has the lower opportunity cost of bread, so Eli has the comparative advantage in bread. Opportunity cost of one jar: Dana gives up 6/12 = 0.5 loaf, Eli gives up 1 loaf, so Dana has the comparative advantage in jam. Specializing accordingly (Dana in jam, Eli in bread) and trading yields gains. The option saying Dana should make both goods confuses absolute with comparative advantage. The option based on Dana's higher loaf output compares quantities instead of opportunity costs. The option saying Eli gives up 1 loaf per jar versus 2 for Dana inverts the ratios (Dana's cost of jam is actually lower). The option denying gains from trade is wrong because opportunity costs differ, so mutually beneficial trade exists.

s3-micro-07.stem: Alpha and Beta can trade, with each producer specializing in the good for which it has the comparative advantage. Based on the table, which of the following exchange rates would make BOTH producers better off than producing each good on their own?

stimulus.description: Table of maximum output per hour of labor for Producer Alpha and Producer Beta in goods X and Y.

columns: Units of X per hour (if all time on X)
Units of Y per hour (if all time on Y)
data.note: Constant opportunity costs; each producer can split time between goods in any proportion.

options.text: Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 1.5 units of X
options.why: Below Alpha's opportunity cost of 2 X per Y, so Alpha gets less X than it gives up; student confused which side benefits or reversed the cost comparison.

options.text: Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 2 units of X
options.why: Equal to Alpha's opportunity cost of Y; Alpha gains nothing. Student treats the boundary as a gain.

options.text: Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 4 units of X
options.why: Equal to Beta's opportunity cost of Y; Beta gains nothing. Student treats the boundary as a gain.

options.text: Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 3 units of X
options.why: Correct: lies strictly between Alpha's opportunity cost (2 X per Y) and Beta's (4 X per Y), so both gain.

options.text: Alpha trades 1 unit of Y to Beta in exchange for 5 units of X
options.why: Above Beta's opportunity cost of 4 X per Y, so Beta would pay more than producing Y itself; student thinks Alpha, with absolute advantage, should get the best terms.

s3-micro-07.explanation_en: Alpha's opportunity cost of 1 Y is 24/12 = 2 X; Beta's is 20/5 = 4 X. Alpha therefore has the comparative advantage in Y (and Beta in X, since 0.25 Y < 0.5 Y), even though Alpha has the absolute advantage in both goods. Alpha specializes in Y and Beta in X. Both gain only if the price of 1 Y is strictly between 2 X and 4 X, and 3 X per Y is the only option in that range. 1.5 X leaves Alpha worse off than making X itself. 2 X leaves Alpha no better off. 4 X leaves Beta no better off. 5 X makes Beta worse off than producing Y itself.

s3-micro-08.stem: Based on the table, which of the following correctly identifies the comparative advantage and a trade that would benefit both clinics?

stimulus.description: Maximum daily output of two services for two telehealth clinics, using all resources on one service.

data.title: Maximum daily output if a clinic devotes all resources to one service
data.assumptions: Constant opportunity costs; each clinic can split resources in any proportion.

options.text: Alpha has the comparative advantage in virtual visits; Alpha trading 1 virtual visit to Beta for 0.4 scan readings benefits both clinics.
options.why: Wrong specialization: Alpha's opportunity cost of a visit is 0.5 scan, higher than Beta's 1/3; also 0.4 scan is in the range, but the premise is wrong since Beta holds the advantage in visits.

options.text: Alpha has the comparative advantage in both services because it can produce more of each; Beta should not trade with Alpha.
options.why: Confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage; it is impossible to have a comparative advantage in both goods.

options.text: Beta has the comparative advantage in scan readings; Beta trading 1 scan reading to Alpha for 2.5 virtual visits benefits both clinics.
options.why: Reverses the opportunity costs: Beta gives up 3 visits per scan, which is higher than Alpha's cost, so Beta does not have the comparative advantage in scans.

options.text: Alpha has the comparative advantage in scan readings; Alpha trading 1 scan reading to Beta for 1.5 virtual visits benefits both clinics.
options.why: Correct specialization but a price outside the mutually beneficial range: 1.5 visits is below Alpha's own opportunity cost of 2, so Alpha loses.

options.text: Alpha has the comparative advantage in scan readings; Alpha trading 1 scan reading to Beta for 2.5 virtual visits benefits both clinics.
options.why: Correct: Alpha's opportunity cost of a scan is 2 visits versus Beta's 3, so Alpha has the comparative advantage in scans, and a price of 2.5 visits per scan lies between 2 and 3.

s3-micro-08.explanation_en: Alpha gives up 20/40 = 0.5 scan per visit, or 2 visits per scan. Beta gives up 10/30 = 1/3 scan per visit, or 3 visits per scan. Alpha has the lower opportunity cost of scans, so it has the comparative advantage in scans, and Beta has it in visits. Both gain if the price of a scan is between 2 and 3 visits, so 2.5 visits works. The option claiming Alpha has the advantage in both services confuses absolute with comparative advantage. The option assigning scans to Beta reverses the opportunity costs. The 1.5-visit price is below Alpha's own cost of 2 visits, so Alpha would be worse off. The option with Alpha specializing in visits misidentifies the advantage, because Alpha's cost per visit (0.5 scan) exceeds Beta's (1/3 scan).

s3-micro-09.stem: A good has the demand function shown, Qd = 50 - 4P + 0.5I. Average income I rises from 40 to 60 while the price stays at $5. Which of the following correctly explains the effect on the quantity consumers buy at $5?

stimulus.description: Abstract demand function for a good, with income I as a determinant.

variables.Qd: quantity demanded in units per week
variables.I: average consumer income in hundreds of dollars per month

data.scenario: I rises from 40 to 60 while P is held at 5 dollars; all other determinants of demand are unchanged

options.text: The demand curve shifts leftward because the good is inferior, so quantity demanded at $5 falls from 50 to 40.
options.why: Misconception: confuses the sign of the income effect and treats a rise in income as lowering demand; also gets the arithmetic wrong.

options.text: The demand curve shifts rightward because the good is normal, so quantity demanded at $5 rises from 50 to 60.
options.why: Correct: the positive income coefficient means the good is normal; the income change shifts demand right, and at P=5 Qd goes from 50 to 60.

options.text: Quantity demanded rises from 50 to 60 as consumers move down along the same demand curve to a lower price.
options.why: Misconception: confuses a shift of demand with a movement along the demand curve; the price did not change.

options.text: The demand curve shifts rightward because the good is normal, so quantity demanded at $5 rises from 30 to 60.
options.why: Misconception: correct direction but an incorrect starting quantity, from mishandling the income term (omitting it or the price term); the initial Qd is 50, not 30.

options.text: The demand curve does not shift because price is unchanged, so quantity demanded at $5 stays at 50.
options.why: Misconception: believes only a price change can change demand, ignoring that non-price determinants such as income shift the curve.

s3-micro-09.explanation_en: At P=5 and I=40, Qd = 50 - 20 + 20 = 50. At I=60, Qd = 50 - 20 + 30 = 60. The positive coefficient on income means the good is normal, and a change in income, a non-price determinant, shifts the whole demand curve rightward. The inferior-good option has the sign of the income effect backwards. The movement-along-the-curve option wrongly treats this as a price change, but the price stayed at $5. The option starting from 30 misstates the initial quantity, which is 50. The no-shift option ignores that non-price determinants such as income shift demand even when price is constant.

s3-micro-10.stem: A bakery owner is considering raising the price of a sourdough loaf from $6 to $8. The table shows weekly quantity demanded at each price. Using the midpoint method, which of the following correctly gives the price elasticity of demand over this price range and the effect of the price increase on the bakery's total revenue?

stimulus.description: Weekly demand for sourdough loaves at a neighborhood bakery at two prices.

data.title: Weekly demand for sourdough loaves

options.text: Elastic, about 1.27; total revenue rises from $720 to $780
options.why: Computes elasticity correctly but applies the revenue rule backward, believing a price increase raises revenue when demand is elastic.

options.text: Inelastic, about 0.79; total revenue rises from $780 to $720
options.why: Inverts the ratio (percent change in price divided by percent change in quantity), getting 0.79, and then also states a revenue rise that does not match the numbers.

options.text: Elastic, about 1.27; total revenue falls from $780 to $720
options.why: Correct: midpoint %change in Q = 40/110 = 36.4%, %change in P = 2/7 = 28.6%, Ed = 1.27 > 1, so a price increase lowers TR from 6x130=780 to 8x90=720.

options.text: Inelastic, about 0.79; total revenue falls from $780 to $720
options.why: Inverts the elasticity ratio to 0.79 but reports the actual revenue change; the label and the revenue result are inconsistent with each other.

options.text: Unit elastic, about 1.00; total revenue stays at $780
options.why: Uses starting-point percentages (about 0.92) and rounds to unit elastic, assuming revenue is unchanged.

s3-micro-10.explanation_en: Midpoint method: percent change in quantity = (90-130)/110 = -36.4%; percent change in price = (8-6)/7 = 28.6%. Elasticity = 36.4/28.6, about 1.27, so demand is elastic. Revenue at $6 is 6 x 130 = $780 and at $8 is 8 x 90 = $720, so revenue falls, consistent with the rule that a price increase lowers revenue when demand is elastic. The inelastic options come from inverting the ratio, and an inelastic result would imply revenue rising, which the numbers contradict. The option pairing elastic with rising revenue reverses the total revenue rule and also misstates the direction of the numbers. The unit elastic option comes from using starting-point percentages and rounding, but the midpoint value is clearly above 1 and revenue does change.

s3-micro-11.stem: The demand for a good is given by Q = 120 - 4P, where Q is units per day and P is price in dollars. The price rises from $10 to $14. Using the midpoint method, which of the following correctly describes the price elasticity of demand over this price range and the effect on total revenue?

stimulus.description: Linear demand equation given in the stem; no figure.

options.text: Elastic, about 4.00; total revenue decreases
options.why: Treats the slope of the demand curve (4) as the elasticity, ignoring the percent changes.

options.text: Elastic, about 1.50; total revenue decreases
options.why: Inverts the ratio (%dP / %dQ = 1.5), then concludes elastic; revenue conclusion is also wrong.

options.text: Inelastic, about 0.50; total revenue decreases
options.why: Uses the initial-point base for both changes: (16/80)/(4/10) = 0.5, and then wrongly says revenue falls for an inelastic good.

options.text: Inelastic, about 0.67; total revenue increases
options.why: Correct: midpoint %dQ = 16/72 = 22.2%, %dP = 4/12 = 33.3%, |E| = 0.67 < 1, so a price increase raises revenue (800 to 896).

options.text: Unit elastic, 1.00; total revenue is unchanged
options.why: Assumes a linear demand curve has constant unit elasticity, ignoring that elasticity varies along the curve.

s3-micro-11.explanation_en: At $10, Q = 80; at $14, Q = 64. Midpoint quantity is 72 and midpoint price is 12. The percent change in quantity is 16/72 = 22.2% and in price is 4/12 = 33.3%, so |E| = 0.67. Demand is inelastic, so the price increase raises total revenue, from 800 to 896. The elastic answer with 1.50 inverts the ratio. The inelastic answer with 0.50 uses starting values instead of midpoints and wrongly says revenue falls. The answer with 4.00 confuses the slope with elasticity. Unit elasticity is wrong because elasticity changes along a linear demand curve.

s3-micro-12.stem: A manufacturer cuts the price of its smartwatch as shown in the table. Using the midpoint method, what is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand over this price range, and what happens to the manufacturer's total revenue?

stimulus.description: Table of price and quantity demanded of a fitness smartwatch before and after a price cut.

data.title: Demand for the StrideBand smartwatch
columns: Quantity demanded (thousands of watches per month)
data.note: Assume the change is a movement along a single demand curve.

options.text: 0.4, demand is inelastic; total revenue falls
options.why: Uses 40% divided by 100% or confuses the percent change in quantity with the elasticity; the revenue conclusion happens to match but the value is wrong.

options.text: 0.8, demand is inelastic; total revenue rises
options.why: Correct elasticity but wrong revenue rule: student thinks a price cut always raises revenue because quantity rises.

options.text: 1.25, demand is elastic; total revenue rises
options.why: Inverts the ratio (%ΔP over %ΔQ) giving 1.25, then applies the right rule for elastic demand with a price cut.

options.text: 1.25, demand is elastic; total revenue falls
options.why: Inverts the ratio to 1.25 and also misapplies the revenue rule for elastic demand.

options.text: 0.8, demand is inelastic; total revenue falls
options.why: Correct: midpoint %ΔQ = 200/500 = 40%, %ΔP = 100/200 = 50%, Ed = 0.8 (<1, inelastic); price falls and demand is inelastic so revenue falls (100,000 to 90,000 thousand dollars).

s3-micro-12.explanation_en: Midpoint method: the percent change in quantity is (600-400)/((600+400)/2) = 200/500 = 40%, and the percent change in price is (150-250)/((150+250)/2) = 100/200 = 50% in absolute value. So the elasticity is 40/50 = 0.8, which is less than 1, so demand is inelastic. With inelastic demand, a price cut lowers total revenue. Check: revenue before is 250 x 400 = 100,000 and after is 150 x 600 = 90,000 (thousand dollars), a decrease. The option saying revenue rises ignores that the quantity gain is proportionally smaller than the price drop. The 1.25 options invert the ratio (price change over quantity change) and so wrongly call demand elastic. The 0.4 option reports only the quantity percent change instead of dividing by the price percent change.

s3-micro-13.stem: A city runs a field experiment in one district. The transit agency raises the bus fare, and researchers record weekly bike-share rides, as shown in the table. Using the midpoint method, which of the following gives the cross-price elasticity of demand for bike-share rides with respect to the bus fare and the correct interpretation?

stimulus.description: Field experiment results: weekly bike-share rides before and after a bus fare increase.

data.title: Field experiment: bus fare change and bike-share use in one city district
data.note: Bike-share price and all other factors held constant during the experiment.

options.text: About +0.50; bus rides and bike-share rides are substitutes
options.why: Uses simple percent changes from the starting values (25%/50%) rather than the midpoint method specified.

options.text: About +1.80; bus rides and bike-share rides are substitutes
options.why: Inverts the ratio (price change over quantity change), giving 1.80 instead of quantity change over price change.

options.text: About -0.56; bus rides and bike-share rides are complements
options.why: Sign error: assigns a negative sign because price rose, and so wrongly concludes complements; quantity actually rose.

options.text: About +0.56; bus rides and bike-share rides are substitutes
options.why: Correct: midpoint % change in quantity 22.2% divided by % change in price 40% = +0.56; positive sign means substitutes.

options.text: About +0.56; bus rides and bike-share rides are complements
options.why: Computes the magnitude correctly but believes a positive cross-price elasticity indicates complements.

s3-micro-13.explanation_en: Midpoint method: the percent change in bike-share rides is (5,000-4,000)/4,500 = 22.2%. The percent change in the bus fare is (3.00-2.00)/2.50 = 40%. Cross-price elasticity = 22.2%/40% = +0.56. A positive value means that a price increase for one good raises demand for the other, so the goods are substitutes. The +1.80 option flips the ratio. The -0.56 complements option assigns the wrong sign, since rides rose when the fare rose. The +0.50 option uses starting-value percent changes instead of the midpoint method. The +0.56 complements option misreads the sign, because complements have negative cross-price elasticity.

s3-micro-14.stem: Harbor Cafe keeps its muffin price unchanged. Using the information in the table and assuming the percentage effects are additive, about how many muffins per week should the cafe expect to sell after both changes occur?

stimulus.description: Table of elasticity estimates and expected changes for a cafe's muffin market.

data.title: Muffin demand at Harbor Cafe (muffin price held constant)
rows: Cross-price elasticity of muffin demand with respect to the price of scones at a rival bakery
Expected change in rival scone price
Expected change in average customer income

options.why: Correct: cross effect 1.5x6=+9% plus income effect 0.5x4=+2% gives +11%; 2,000 x 1.11 = 2,220.
Counts only the cross-price effect (+9%) and ignores the income change.
Counts only the income effect (+2%) and ignores the rival's price change.
Treats the goods as complements, making the cross effect negative (-9%+2%=-7%), although the positive sign means substitutes.
Adds the two elasticities (2.0) and applies them to the 6% price change only, giving 12% and ignoring the income change's own percentage.

s3-micro-14.explanation_en: The positive cross-price elasticity means muffins and scones are substitutes, so a 6% rise in the scone price raises muffin demand by 1.5 x 6 = 9%. The positive income elasticity means muffins are a normal good, so a 4% income rise adds 0.5 x 4 = 2%. The total is +11%, so sales are 2,000 x 1.11 = 2,220. The 2,180 option leaves out the income effect. The 2,040 option leaves out the cross-price effect. The 1,860 option wrongly treats the goods as complements by making the cross effect negative. The 2,240 option adds the elasticities and applies the sum to only the price change, which misapplies each elasticity to its own percentage change.

s3-micro-15.stem: The market organizers require all vendors to sell bouquets at a fixed price of $3 each, and vendors comply. Based on the table, which of the following correctly describes the outcome in this market each week?

stimulus.description: Table of weekly bunches of flowers demanded and supplied at five prices at a farmers market.

data.title: Weekly market for bouquets at a farmers market

options.text: A surplus of 25 bouquets, with 90 bouquets actually sold
options.why: Misconception: mislabels the gap as a surplus and also uses quantity demanded as the amount sold.

options.text: A shortage of 25 bouquets, with 90 bouquets actually sold
options.why: Misconception: believes that quantity demanded is what actually gets traded during a shortage, ignoring that sellers supply only 65.

options.text: A shortage of 25 bouquets, with 65 bouquets actually sold
options.why: Correct: at $3, quantity demanded is 90 and quantity supplied is 65, so a shortage of 25 exists; only 65 can be sold (the short side).

options.text: A surplus of 25 bouquets, with 65 bouquets actually sold
options.why: Misconception: confuses which side exceeds the other at a price below equilibrium, calling the gap a surplus although the quantity sold is correctly the supplied amount.

options.text: No shortage or surplus, with 80 bouquets actually sold
options.why: Misconception: assumes the market always reaches equilibrium even when the price is fixed below the equilibrium price of $4.

s3-micro-15.explanation_en: The equilibrium price is $4 (quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at 80). At the fixed price of $3, quantity demanded is 90 and quantity supplied is 65, so there is a shortage of 90 - 65 = 25 bouquets. Because the price cannot rise, trade is limited by the smaller quantity, so 65 bouquets are sold. The option with 90 sold is wrong because sellers will not supply more than 65 at $3. The options calling the gap a surplus are wrong because a price below equilibrium makes demand exceed supply. The option with no shortage and 80 sold is wrong because the fixed price prevents the market from moving to equilibrium.

s3-micro-16.stem: The table shows the market for single-game tickets at a minor-league arena. Before the signing, the city had set a binding price ceiling of $20 per ticket and it remains in force. After the star player signs, demand increases to the schedule shown. What is the resulting situation in the ticket market at the $20 ceiling?

stimulus.description: Table of ticket prices with quantity demanded before and after a star player signs, and quantity supplied, for a minor-league arena.

data.title: Single-game tickets for a minor-league arena
data.units: price in dollars, quantity in tickets

options.text: A shortage of 600 tickets
options.why: Subtracts the old equilibrium quantity from the new equilibrium quantity (6,800 - 6,200), confusing the change in equilibrium with the shortage at the ceiling.

options.text: A shortage of 2,000 tickets
options.why: Uses the pre-signing demand schedule (7,000 - 5,000) and ignores the demand increase.

options.text: A shortage of 5,000 tickets
options.why: Reports the quantity supplied at the ceiling as the shortage instead of subtracting it from quantity demanded.

options.text: A shortage of 3,000 tickets
options.why: Correct: at $20, quantity demanded after the signing is 8,000 and quantity supplied is 5,000, so the shortage is 3,000.

options.text: A shortage of 8,000 tickets
options.why: Reports the quantity demanded at the ceiling as the shortage instead of subtracting quantity supplied.

s3-micro-16.explanation_en: The new equilibrium price is $32, so the $20 ceiling is still below it and binds. At $20, quantity demanded on the new schedule is 8,000 and quantity supplied is 5,000, so the shortage is 3,000 tickets. The 2,000 option uses the old demand and ignores the shift. The 600 option compares equilibrium quantities rather than quantities at the ceiling. The 5,000 and 8,000 options report one side of the market rather than the gap between quantity demanded and quantity supplied.

s3-micro-17.stem: The graph shows the market for cacao beans in a small country that can import any amount at the world price. The government imposes a tariff of $10 per kg. Compared with free trade, which of the following correctly describes the outcome?

stimulus.description: Market for cacao beans in a small country: downward-sloping domestic demand, upward-sloping domestic supply, horizontal world price line at $40 per kg, and a higher line at $50 per kg after a $10 tariff.

data.notes: Small country takes the world price as given; the tariff is a $10 per kg tax on each imported kg.

options.text: Imports fall from 20 to 10 thousand kg, and the government collects $100 thousand in tariff revenue.
options.why: Correct: price rises to $50, Qd=25, Qs=15, imports=10, revenue=10x10=100.

options.text: Imports fall from 20 to 10 thousand kg, and the government collects $200 thousand in tariff revenue.
options.why: Multiplies the tariff by free-trade imports (20) instead of post-tariff imports (10).

options.text: Imports fall from 20 to 0 thousand kg, because the tariff raises the domestic price above the world price.
options.why: Believes any tariff above zero eliminates imports; confuses a tariff with a ban, ignoring that the $50 price is still below the autarky price of $60.

options.text: Imports fall from 20 to 10 thousand kg, and domestic consumers pay the world price of $40 while producers receive $50.
options.why: Thinks consumers and producers face different prices; with a tariff both face the same domestic price of $50.

options.text: Imports stay at 20 thousand kg, because the tariff is paid by foreign exporters and does not change domestic prices.
options.why: Thinks a small country's tariff is paid by foreign exporters and leaves domestic price and imports unchanged.

s3-micro-17.explanation_en: Under free trade the domestic price is the world price of $40. Demand gives Qd = 30 and supply gives Qs = 10, so imports are 20. The $10 tariff raises the domestic price to $50, so Qd = 25 and Qs = 15 and imports fall to 10. Revenue is $10 x 10 = $100 thousand, so the first option is correct. Revenue of $200 thousand wrongly uses the pre-tariff import quantity. Imports do not fall to zero, because the autarky price is $60, which is above $50, so trade continues. The option with different prices for consumers and producers is wrong because both face the single domestic price of $50. The claim that imports are unchanged is wrong because a small country faces a fixed world price, so the tariff raises the domestic price and reduces imports.

s3-micro-18.stem: A firm uses a fixed amount of capital and hires identical workers. The table shows the firm's total product at each level of labor. Which of the following correctly describes the production function shown?

stimulus.description: Table of workers and total product for a firm with fixed capital.

data.note: Capital is fixed; all workers are identical.

options.text: Total product begins to fall after the fifth worker, so diminishing marginal returns begin with the sixth worker.
options.why: Misconception: equates diminishing marginal returns with falling total product (negative marginal product); total product here never falls.

options.text: Marginal product rises through the third worker and then falls, so diminishing marginal returns begin with the fourth worker.
options.why: Misconception: confuses the point where total product's growth slows (third worker's total of 44) or off-by-one error in reading marginal product by the worker count rather than the change.

options.text: Marginal product falls from the first worker onward, so diminishing marginal returns begin with the first worker.
options.why: Misconception: assumes diminishing returns apply from the start, ignoring that the second worker adds more (18) than the first (12).

options.text: Marginal product rises through the second worker and then falls, so diminishing marginal returns begin with the third worker.
options.why: Correct: MP is 12, 18, 14, 10, 6, 2; the maximum is at the second worker, and MP declines starting with the third worker.

options.text: Average product is constant across all workers, so the firm experiences constant returns to labor throughout.
options.why: Misconception: confuses constant total product increments with constant returns; average product is 12, 15, 14.7, 13.5, 12, 10.3, not constant.

s3-micro-18.explanation_en: Marginal product is the change in total product per added worker: 12, 18, 14, 10, 6, 2. It rises through the second worker and falls beginning with the third, so diminishing marginal returns begin with the third worker. The option placing the onset at the fourth worker misreads where MP first declines. The option claiming diminishing returns from the first worker ignores that the second worker adds more than the first. The option tying diminishing returns to falling total product confuses diminishing marginal product with negative marginal product; total product keeps rising through the sixth worker. The option claiming constant returns is wrong because neither marginal nor average product is constant.

s3-micro-19.stem: A sports rehabilitation clinic has 4 treatment tables that cannot be changed in the short run. The table shows how many patients the clinic treats per day as it hires more therapists. Which of the following correctly describes the production function shown?

stimulus.description: Table of daily patients treated at a physical therapy clinic with a fixed number of treatment tables (4) and different numbers of therapists.

data.title: Sports Rehab Clinic: Daily Output (4 treatment tables, fixed)

options.text: Total product rises at a constant rate because each therapist adds the same number of patients.
options.why: Misconception: ignores the marginal calculation; the increments (8, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2) are not constant.

options.text: Total product rises throughout, and the marginal product of a therapist begins to fall after the first therapist.
options.why: Misconception: assumes diminishing returns start immediately; the 2nd therapist adds 10, more than the 1st adds (8), so MP rises at first.

options.text: Total product begins to fall after the fifth therapist because the marginal product becomes negative.
options.why: Misconception: confuses diminishing marginal returns with negative marginal returns; MP falls to 2 but stays positive, so total product still rises.

options.text: Total product rises at an increasing rate throughout because each added therapist treats more patients in total.
options.why: Misconception: confuses a rising total product with an increasing marginal product; MP actually falls after the 2nd therapist.

options.text: Total product rises throughout, and the marginal product of a therapist begins to fall after the second therapist.
options.why: Correct: MP is 8, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2; it peaks with the 2nd therapist and falls afterward, while total product keeps rising.

s3-micro-19.explanation_en: Marginal product is the change in total product from one more therapist: 8, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. It rises from the first to the second therapist, then falls beginning with the third, so diminishing marginal returns set in after the second therapist, while total product keeps increasing (just more slowly). The option claiming diminishing returns after the first therapist is wrong because the second therapist adds more (10) than the first (8). The option claiming total product falls after the fifth therapist is wrong because the sixth still adds 2 patients; MP is falling but positive. The option claiming total product rises at an increasing rate is wrong because rising total product does not mean rising marginal product; the increments shrink after the second therapist. The option claiming a constant rate is wrong because the increments differ.

s3-micro-20.stem: A bakery owner uses the table to compare a short-run cost model (oven size fixed) with a long-run cost model (oven size chosen). Which statement correctly identifies a difference between the two models, based on the table?

stimulus.description: Average total cost (dollars per loaf) of a bakery at several output levels for three possible oven sizes. A dash means the plant size is not considered at that output.

data.title: Average total cost per loaf by plant size
data.note: Each plant size has a fixed oven size in the short run. In the long run the bakery can choose any of the three plant sizes before producing.

options.text: At 200 loaves, the long-run model gives $10 per loaf because the bakery must keep the plant size that it used at the lowest output level.
options.why: Believes the bakery is locked into its earliest plant choice in the long run; that is the short-run constraint, and at 200 the long-run cost is $9 (medium).

options.text: At 100 loaves, the long-run model gives $14 per loaf because the medium plant is the most advanced technology available.
options.why: Confuses a larger or newer plant with lower cost; the long-run model picks the lowest-cost plant, which at 100 loaves is small at $12.

options.text: At 300 loaves, the long-run model gives $13 per loaf because the long-run cost must equal the average of all three plants' costs.
options.why: Thinks long-run cost is an average of plant costs rather than the minimum; the lowest at 300 is $8 (medium).

options.text: At 500 loaves, the long-run model gives $9 per loaf only because the large plant has fixed costs that are lower than the other plants' fixed costs.
options.why: Attributes the long-run cost to lower fixed costs; in the long run all inputs are variable and the cost is simply the lowest available, and the table gives no fixed cost data.

options.text: At 400 loaves, the short-run model with the medium plant gives $10 per loaf, while the long-run model allows $9.50 by switching to the large plant.
options.why: Correct: long-run cost at each output is the lowest cost across plant sizes, so at 400 loaves it is $9.50 (large) rather than $10 for the fixed medium plant.

s3-micro-20.explanation_en: The long-run model lets the firm choose the plant size, so the long-run average total cost at each output is the lowest ATC among the available plants. At 400 loaves, the medium plant (fixed in the short run) costs $10, but the large plant costs $9.50, so long-run cost is $9.50. The $14 claim is wrong because the long-run cost at 100 loaves is $12 from the small plant; newer or larger does not mean cheaper. The $13 claim is wrong because long-run cost is the minimum, not an average; at 300 it is $8. The $9 claim at 500 is right as a number, but the stated reason is wrong: the table says nothing about fixed costs, and the long-run cost is the lowest available cost rather than a result of lower fixed costs. The $10 claim at 200 is wrong because the bakery is not locked into a plant in the long run; the lowest cost at 200 is $9 with the medium plant.

s3-micro-21.stem: The table gives a firm's long-run average total cost (LRATC) at five output levels. Which of the following correctly compares this long-run cost model with a short-run cost model, as applied to the data?

stimulus.description: Long-run average total cost at five output levels, with all inputs variable.

columns: Long-run average total cost (dollars per unit)
data.notes: All inputs, including plant size, can be changed at every output level shown.

options.text: The fall in LRATC from 10 to 30 units reflects diminishing marginal returns, because adding inputs lowers the average cost per unit.
options.why: Confuses economies of scale with diminishing marginal returns, which is a short-run concept with a fixed input.

options.text: The rise in LRATC from 40 to 50 units reflects economies of scale ending, whereas short-run rising cost reflects diminishing marginal returns to a fixed input.
options.why: Correct: it identifies rising LRATC as diseconomies of scale (the end of scale economies), distinct from the short-run source of rising costs, diminishing returns to a fixed input.

options.text: The rise in LRATC from 40 to 50 units shows that marginal cost is below LRATC there, which pulls the average up.
options.why: Misapplies the average-marginal rule: an average rises only when marginal cost is above it, not below it.

options.text: The flat LRATC from 30 to 40 units shows diseconomies of scale, because average cost no longer falls when output increases.
options.why: Confuses constant returns to scale (flat LRATC) with diseconomies of scale (rising LRATC).

options.text: The table cannot show scale effects, because the long-run model holds plant size fixed and varies only labor.
options.why: Reverses the models: the long-run model has all inputs variable, and the short-run model holds plant size fixed.

s3-micro-21.explanation_en: The long-run model lets every input vary, so changes in LRATC show returns to scale. LRATC falls from 10 to 30 units (economies of scale), is flat from 30 to 40 (constant returns to scale), and rises from 40 to 50 (diseconomies of scale). The short-run model has a fixed input, so rising short-run costs come from diminishing marginal returns. That is why the statement that the rise after 40 units marks the end of scale economies, in contrast with short-run diminishing returns, is correct. The statement that the fall from 10 to 30 units reflects diminishing returns is wrong, because falling LRATC is economies of scale and diminishing returns is a short-run, fixed-input idea. The statement that marginal cost is below LRATC when LRATC rises is wrong, because an average rises only when marginal cost is above it. The statement that the flat segment shows diseconomies is wrong, because flat LRATC is constant returns to scale. The statement that the long-run model holds plant size fixed is wrong, because all inputs, including plant size, are variable in the long run.

s3-micro-22.stem: The table shows one year of data for a soil-testing lab that is owned and run by one person. Based on the table, the lab's economic profit for the year is

stimulus.description: Annual revenue, explicit costs, and owner's forgone earnings for a soil-testing lab.

data.title: Prairie Soil Testing Lab, one year
rows: Salary owner gave up by running the lab instead of working elsewhere
Owner's own savings invested in the lab
Annual return those savings would earn in their best alternative use (6%)

options.why: Misconception: confuses normal profit (the implicit costs, the owner's opportunity cost) with economic profit.
Misconception: treats accounting profit (revenue minus explicit costs only) as economic profit, ignoring implicit costs.
Correct: revenue 180,000 minus explicit costs 120,000 minus implicit costs 51,000 (45,000 salary + 6,000 forgone interest) = 9,000.
Misconception: subtracts forgone salary but forgets the forgone return on the owner's invested savings as an implicit cost.
Misconception: double-counts the forgone interest (subtracts it twice) when accounting for implicit costs.

s3-micro-22.explanation_en: Explicit costs are 70,000 + 30,000 + 20,000 = 120,000, so accounting profit is 180,000 - 120,000 = 60,000. Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs: the 45,000 forgone salary and the 6,000 forgone return on the owner's savings, 51,000 in total. Economic profit is 60,000 - 51,000 = 9,000. The 60,000 figure is only accounting profit because it ignores implicit costs. The 51,000 figure is the normal profit (the owner's opportunity cost), not a profit above it. The 15,000 figure leaves out the forgone return on the owner's savings. The 3,000 figure subtracts the forgone interest twice.

s3-micro-23.stem: Based on the table, which of the following correctly describes the firm's profit situation?

stimulus.description: Annual revenue and cost figures for a firm, in thousands of dollars.

data.title: Annual figures for a firm (thousands of dollars)

options.text: Accounting profit is -30 and economic profit is -30, so the firm earns less than a normal profit.
options.why: Misconception: subtracts implicit costs for both measures, so accounting profit wrongly includes implicit costs.

options.text: Accounting profit is 180 and economic profit is 180, so the firm earns more than a normal profit.
options.why: Misconception: ignores implicit costs when computing economic profit, treating it as equal to accounting profit.

options.text: Accounting profit is -30 and economic profit is 180, so the firm earns more than a normal profit.
options.why: Misconception: reverses the two definitions, subtracting implicit costs for accounting profit and only explicit for economic profit.

options.text: Accounting profit is 180 and economic profit is -30, so the firm earns less than a normal profit.
options.why: Correct: accounting profit = 500-320 = 180; economic profit = 500-(320+210) = -30 < 0, meaning less than normal profit.

options.text: Accounting profit is 180 and economic profit is 0, so the firm earns exactly a normal profit.
options.why: Misconception: believes positive accounting profit implies zero economic profit (normal profit) without subtracting implicit costs.

s3-micro-23.explanation_en: Accounting profit subtracts only explicit costs: 500 - 320 = 180. Economic profit subtracts explicit and implicit costs: 500 - 530 = -30. Negative economic profit means the owners earn less than their opportunity cost, i.e., less than a normal profit. The option saying both measures equal 180 ignores implicit costs. The option reversing the definitions mixes up which costs each measure includes. The option with both measures at -30 wrongly deducts implicit costs from accounting profit. The option claiming zero economic profit confuses positive accounting profit with normal profit.

s3-micro-24.stem: Based on the table, which statement correctly identifies the firm's profit?

stimulus.description: Annual revenue and costs for a one-owner fitness-app company.

data.title: Annual figures, FitPulse App Studio (owner-operated)
rows: Salary the owner could earn working elsewhere (not paid by the firm)
Owner's own funds invested in the firm
Annual return the owner's funds could earn in their next-best use (6%)

options.text: Economic profit is $20,000, so the firm earns more than the owner's opportunity costs.
options.why: Correct: explicit costs 310,000, implicit costs 150,000, economic profit 480,000-460,000=20,000 >0.

options.text: Economic profit is $170,000, because it equals revenue minus the costs the firm actually paid.
options.why: Confuses economic profit with accounting profit by ignoring implicit costs.

options.text: Economic profit is $0, because the owner's forgone salary and return are the normal profit.
options.why: Confuses normal profit (the implicit costs) with zero economic profit; assumes covering implicit costs means no profit remains.

options.text: Economic profit is -$130,000, because implicit costs are subtracted from revenue along with explicit costs and accounting profit.
options.why: Double counts by subtracting the implicit costs from accounting profit and also treating explicit costs again, giving a wrong negative value.

options.text: Normal profit is $170,000, because it equals the firm's accounting profit.
options.why: Confuses normal profit with accounting profit; normal profit is the 150,000 of implicit costs.

s3-micro-24.explanation_en: Explicit costs are 210,000+60,000+40,000=310,000, so accounting profit is 480,000-310,000=170,000. Implicit costs are the owner's forgone salary of 120,000 plus the forgone 6% return on 500,000 (30,000), or 150,000. Economic profit is 170,000-150,000=20,000, which is positive, so the firm earns more than all of its opportunity costs. The option giving 170,000 as economic profit ignores implicit costs. The zero-profit option mistakes covering implicit costs (normal profit) for having no profit left over; here 20,000 remains. The negative option subtracts costs twice and yields an incorrect figure. The normal-profit option confuses normal profit with accounting profit, since normal profit is the implicit-cost amount of 150,000.

s3-micro-25.stem: A small bakery is a price taker and sells each loaf for $6.50. The table shows its total cost at each daily output. The bakery is currently baking 6 loaves per day. Based on the table, what should the bakery do to maximize profit?

stimulus.description: Table of daily output and total cost for a bakery selling loaves at a constant market price of $6.50 per loaf.

options.text: Increase output above 6 loaves per day, because the price is higher than the marginal cost of the first loaf
options.why: Misconception: compares price to the MC of the first unit instead of the marginal unit; MC of the 6th loaf is $8, above the price.

options.text: Keep producing 6 loaves per day, because total revenue of $39 is greater than the $10 fixed cost
options.why: Misconception: compares total revenue to fixed cost only and ignores variable cost and marginal reasoning; the 5th and 6th loaves cost more than they bring in.

options.text: Reduce output to 3 loaves per day, because that is where marginal cost is closest to average total cost
options.why: Misconception: confuses the MC=ATC point with the profit-maximizing rule MR=MC; at 3 loaves MC ($5) is still below the price, so profit can still rise.

options.text: Shut down and produce 0 loaves, because the bakery is earning a negative economic profit at 6 loaves
options.why: Misconception: assumes any loss means shutting down; revenue at 4 loaves ($26) exceeds variable cost ($20), so the loss ($4) is smaller than the fixed cost ($10).

options.text: Reduce output to 4 loaves per day, because the marginal cost of the 5th loaf exceeds $6.50
options.why: Correct: MR=P=6.50; the 4th loaf has MC $6 < $6.50 so it adds profit, the 5th has MC $7 > $6.50 so it reduces profit; the best output is 4, with a loss of $4 smaller than the $10 loss from shutting down.

s3-micro-25.explanation_en: A price-taking firm maximizes profit by producing until marginal cost reaches price. Marginal costs are $5, $4, $5, $6, $7, $8 for loaves 1 to 6. The 4th loaf (MC $6) costs less than the $6.50 it earns, so it raises profit. The 5th loaf (MC $7) costs more than $6.50, so it lowers profit. The bakery should therefore cut output from 6 to 4 loaves. Profit at 4 loaves is $26 - $30 = -$4, better than -$4.50 at 5, -$6 at 6, and -$10 at zero output (fixed cost only). Keeping 6 loaves because revenue exceeds fixed cost ignores that the extra loaves cost more than they earn. Stopping at 3 loaves uses the MC=ATC idea and forgoes a profitable 4th loaf. Shutting down is wrong because revenue covers variable cost, so the loss is smaller than the fixed cost. Expanding beyond 6 is wrong because MC of the 6th loaf is already $8, above the price.

s3-micro-26.stem: A fitness-tracker assembler is a price taker and currently produces 6 units per day. Based on the table, what should the firm do to maximize profit, and why?

stimulus.description: Marginal cost schedule for a fitness-tracker assembler selling in a perfectly competitive market at a price of $40 per unit.

data.market_structure: perfectly competitive, firm is a price taker
data.fixed_cost_note: Average total cost at 6 units is $38 per unit

options.text: Keep output at 6 units, because price is greater than average total cost, so the firm earns a profit
options.why: Misconception: confuses earning a positive profit with maximizing profit; P > ATC does not mean output is optimal when MC > MR.

options.text: Reduce output to 4 units, because the 5th and 6th units each add more to cost than to revenue
options.why: Correct: a price taker's MR equals the price of $40; units 5 (MC $44) and 6 (MC $55) cost more than the $40 they bring in, so output of 4 is optimal.

options.text: Reduce output to 1 unit, because marginal cost is lowest there and so profit per unit is greatest
options.why: Misconception: maximizing profit per unit instead of total profit; ignores that every unit with MC below price adds to profit.

options.text: Increase output above 6 units, because price exceeds average total cost and more output adds more profit
options.why: Misconception: thinks more output always raises profit when P > ATC; ignores that MC exceeds MR beyond 4 units.

options.text: Reduce output to 5 units, because the 5th unit is the first one whose marginal cost exceeds the price
options.why: Misconception: correctly spots that unit 5 has MC above price but then stops at 5 units, counting that unit as acceptable instead of cutting it. Producing the 5th unit costs $44 and earns only $40.

s3-micro-26.explanation_en: For a price-taking firm, marginal revenue equals the price, $40. Profit rises with each unit whose marginal cost is at most $40 (units 1 to 4, with MC of 15, 20, 28 and 36). Unit 5 has MC of $44 and unit 6 has MC of $55, both above the $40 of added revenue, so each lowers profit. The firm should cut output to 4 units, where MR = MC is satisfied as closely as the discrete units allow. Keeping output at 6 units because price exceeds average total cost confuses being profitable with maximizing profit. Cutting to 1 unit because marginal cost is lowest there ignores the profitable units 2 through 4. Expanding beyond 6 units adds units that cost even more than the price. Stopping at 5 units keeps a unit that costs $44 but earns only $40.

s3-micro-27.stem: A small bakery sells identical loaves in a perfectly competitive market at a price of $14 per loaf. The table shows its daily total cost schedule. In the short run, which action should the bakery take, and why?

stimulus.description: Cost schedule for a price-taking firm: output, total cost and marginal cost, with a market price of $14.

data.note: Total cost at zero output ($30) is a fixed cost that cannot be avoided in the short run.

options.text: Shut down, because the price of $14 is below the average total cost of $17.50 at 4 loaves and the firm cannot earn an economic profit
options.why: Misconception: shutting down whenever P < ATC; ignores that fixed cost is sunk and P exceeds AVC (10), so shutdown loses 30 versus 14.

options.text: Produce 5 loaves, because the price of $14 is above the average variable cost at that quantity and so total revenue is maximized there
options.why: Misconception: producing until P exceeds AVC rather than comparing P with MC at the margin; the 5th unit costs 16 but adds only 14 to revenue.

options.text: Produce 4 loaves, because marginal cost is below the price up to that quantity and the resulting loss is smaller than the $30 fixed cost it would lose by shutting down
options.why: Correct: MR=P=14 exceeds MC through the 4th unit (MC=12) but not the 5th (MC=16); revenue 56 exceeds variable cost 40, so the loss of 14 is less than the fixed cost of 30.

options.text: Produce 3 loaves, because the price of $14 is closest to the average total cost at that quantity, so the loss is as small as possible
options.why: Misconception: choosing output where P is nearest ATC instead of using the MR=MC rule; units 4 still add more revenue than cost.

options.text: Produce 4 loaves, because at that quantity the firm earns zero economic profit when price equals marginal cost
options.why: Misconception: believing P=MC implies zero economic profit; that holds only in long-run equilibrium, here P is below ATC and profit is -14.

s3-micro-27.explanation_en: Marginal costs are 10, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20 for units 1 through 6. A price-taker's marginal revenue equals the price of $14, so each unit through the 4th (MC = 12) adds more to revenue than to cost, while the 5th (MC = 16) does not. At 4 loaves revenue is $56 and total cost is $70, a loss of $14. Shutting down would lose the $30 fixed cost, and since price ($14) exceeds average variable cost ($10), the bakery covers its variable costs and should keep producing at a smaller loss. Producing 5 loaves adds a unit costing more than it earns. Shutting down because price is below average total cost ignores that the fixed cost is unavoidable. Producing 3 loaves forgoes a 4th unit that adds $2 of profit. Zero economic profit at P = MC is a long-run result and does not hold here, since the bakery loses $14.

s3-micro-28.stem: Maria owns the only bakery in a small town and is deciding whether to raise the price of her bread. A friend suggests she analyze her decision using the perfectly competitive model because it is the simplest model. Based on the table, which of the following is the best description of a limitation of using that model for Maria's decision?

stimulus.description: Table comparing characteristics of four market structures: number of sellers, product type, entry barriers, and whether a firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve.

options.text: The model assumes the firm faces a perfectly elastic demand curve, but Maria's demand curve slopes downward, so raising price would not cause her to lose all sales.
options.why: Correct: perfect competition treats each firm as a price taker facing perfectly elastic demand; the only bakery in town has market power and a downward-sloping demand curve, so the model misrepresents her pricing decision.

options.text: The model assumes a differentiated product, but Maria sells an identical product, so she has no ability to set price.
options.why: Confuses product type: perfect competition assumes identical products, not differentiated, and the bakery is not described as selling an identical product.

options.text: The model assumes high barriers to entry, but Maria faces no competitors, so profit would be driven to zero.
options.why: Reverses the model's entry assumption (perfect competition has no barriers) and wrongly attributes zero profit to the absence of competitors.

options.text: The model assumes a few large sellers, but Maria is the only seller, so her pricing depends on rivals' responses.
options.why: Describes oligopoly characteristics (few sellers, interdependence), not the perfectly competitive model; a single seller has no rivals to respond to.

options.text: The model assumes the firm earns zero economic profit in the short run, but Maria can earn positive profit only if she is a monopolist.
options.why: Misstates the model: zero profit is a long-run result in perfect competition, and monopolistic competition and oligopoly firms can also earn positive profit.

s3-micro-28.explanation_en: The perfectly competitive model assumes many sellers of identical products with no entry barriers, so each firm is a price taker facing perfectly elastic demand. Maria is the only seller in town, so she faces a downward-sloping demand curve and can choose her price, trading off a higher price against fewer units sold. The model therefore cannot capture her decision, and this is its key limitation here. The option claiming the model assumes differentiated products is wrong because perfect competition assumes identical products. The option claiming the model assumes high entry barriers is wrong because perfect competition assumes none, and zero profit is a long-run result, not a consequence of having no competitors. The option claiming the model assumes a few large sellers describes oligopoly, and a lone seller has no rivals whose responses matter. The option about zero short-run profit misstates the model, since zero economic profit is a long-run outcome and other imperfectly competitive firms can also earn profit.

s3-micro-29.stem: A laboratory is the only supplier of a specialty enzyme and charges one price to all buyers. Using the table, the lab sells 20 units at $60 rather than expanding to 40 units, where price equals marginal cost. Which statement best explains why the lab stops at 20 units?

stimulus.description: Demand schedule for a sole producer of a specialty enzyme, with constant marginal cost of $20 per unit.

data.note: Firm is the only seller; it must charge one price to all buyers.

options.text: Selling a 21st unit would push the price below $60, and any price below $60 would be below average total cost.
options.why: Misconception: assumes the stopping rule is about covering average cost; no ATC data is given and the P>MC logic is MR-based.

options.text: Selling a 21st unit requires cutting the price on all units, so marginal revenue from it falls below its $20 marginal cost.
options.why: Correct: MR = 100 - 4Q is below price; at Q=21 MR is about 18 < MC of 20, so profit would fall.

options.text: At 20 units the price of $60 exceeds marginal cost, so the lab earns the maximum possible profit per unit.
options.why: Misconception: confuses maximizing profit per unit with maximizing total profit; the rule is MR = MC.

options.text: Selling a 21st unit would raise marginal cost above $60, which is the price at 20 units.
options.why: Misconception: believes marginal cost rises; the table says MC is constant at $20.

options.text: At 20 units total revenue is at its maximum, so selling more units would reduce total revenue.
options.why: Misconception: confuses profit maximization with revenue maximization; revenue peaks where MR = 0 (Q = 25), beyond 20.

s3-micro-29.explanation_en: The lab faces a downward-sloping demand curve and charges a single price, so to sell another unit it must lower the price on every unit. Marginal revenue is therefore below price: MR = 100 - 4Q, which equals 20 at Q = 20 and about 18 for the 21st unit, below the constant MC of $20. Profit is maximized at 20 units. The ATC option fails because no cost data supports it and the stopping rule is MR = MC. The per-unit-profit option confuses profit per unit with total profit. The rising-MC option contradicts the constant $20 MC. The revenue-maximizing option is wrong because total revenue keeps rising until MR = 0 at Q = 25, so revenue is still rising at 20 units.

s3-micro-30.stem: A ferry company is the only provider of service across a bay and charges one price to all riders. It currently runs 6 trips per hour, as shown in the table. Which action should the company take to increase its profit, and why?

stimulus.description: Demand schedule and marginal cost for a single-price ferry monopolist.

options.text: Increase trips, because marginal revenue of $16 exceeds marginal cost of $8 at 6 trips
options.why: Correct: at 6 trips MR 16 > MC 8, so each added trip adds more revenue than cost; the firm should expand until MR = MC at 8 trips.

options.text: Decrease trips, because the price of $28 is well above marginal cost of $8 at 6 trips
options.why: Misconception: compares price rather than marginal revenue with MC; for a monopolist MR is below price, and MR still exceeds MC here.

options.text: Keep 6 trips, because the price of $28 exceeds the cost of each trip and profit is positive
options.why: Misconception: assumes positive profit means maximum profit; profit can still rise while MR > MC.

options.text: Increase trips until the price falls to $8, where price equals marginal cost
options.why: Misconception: applies the perfectly competitive P = MC rule; a monopolist stops where MR = MC, at a price of $24.

options.text: Decrease trips to raise the price, because demand is inelastic at 6 trips
options.why: Misconception: misreads elasticity; at 6 trips elasticity is about 2.3 (elastic), and cutting output when MR > 0 would lower revenue.

s3-micro-30.explanation_en: The profit-maximizing monopolist produces where MR = MC. At 6 trips MR is $16 and MC is $8, so each additional trip adds $8 to profit, and the firm should expand to 8 trips (price $24). Decreasing trips because price exceeds MC is wrong, since the relevant comparison is MR, not price, and MR is still above MC. Keeping 6 trips because profit is positive is wrong, because profit is not yet maximized. Expanding until price equals MC is the competitive rule and would push output to 16 trips, where MR is negative. Claiming demand is inelastic is wrong: MR is positive at 6 trips, which means demand is elastic there, so cutting output would reduce revenue.

s3-micro-31.stem: A single-price monopolist faces the inverse demand P = 100 - 2Q and has constant marginal cost MC = 20 with no fixed cost. The monopolist produces 20 units and charges $60, even though consumers would value each unit up to the 40th at or above MC. Which statement best explains why the monopolist does not expand output to 40 units?

stimulus.description: A single-price monopolist faces a linear demand curve and constant marginal cost.

data.units: P in dollars per unit, Q in units

options.text: Beyond 20 units, average total cost rises above the price, so the monopolist would earn negative economic profit.
options.why: Misconception: treats the stopping rule as ATC versus price; ATC = 20 here (no fixed cost), below price, and the profit-maximizing rule uses marginal values.

options.text: Beyond 20 units, the price falls below marginal cost, so each additional unit is sold at a loss.
options.why: Misconception: confuses price with marginal revenue; at Q = 21 the price is 58, still well above MC = 20.

options.text: Beyond 20 units, marginal cost rises above the demand price, so additional units cannot be sold profitably.
options.why: Misconception: assumes MC rises; MC is constant at 20 and the demand price exceeds it up to Q = 40.

options.text: Beyond 20 units, marginal revenue falls below marginal cost, because selling more requires lowering the price on all units sold.
options.why: Correct: MR = 100 - 4Q equals MC = 20 at Q = 20 and is below MC beyond that, since the price cut applies to all units.

options.text: Beyond 20 units, marginal revenue is negative, so total revenue would fall as soon as output rises past 20 units.
options.why: Misconception: MR is positive until Q = 25, so revenue still rises past 20; MR just falls below MC.

s3-micro-31.explanation_en: MR = 100 - 4Q. Setting MR = MC gives 100 - 4Q = 20, so Q = 20 and P = 60. Past 20 units each extra unit adds less to revenue than it costs, because lowering the price to sell more applies to every unit sold, so MR lies below the demand curve and below MC. The price-below-MC option is wrong because the price stays above MC (58 at Q = 21), so the gap is in MR, not P. The rising-MC option is wrong because MC is constant at 20. The ATC option is wrong because ATC equals 20 and is below the price. The negative-MR option is wrong because MR stays positive until Q = 25, so revenue is still rising at Q = 21.

s3-micro-32.stem: A firm is the only producer of a patented wearable glucose-monitor patch and must charge one price to all buyers. The graph shows its demand, marginal revenue, and constant marginal cost. The firm is currently producing 20 thousand patches per month and selling them at $80 each. Which action should the firm take to increase profit, and why?

stimulus.description: Linear demand curve for a wearable glucose-monitor patch with a constant marginal cost line, plus the marginal revenue curve, for a single-price monopolist.

options.text: Decrease output to raise the price, because a monopolist maximizes profit by restricting output to the inelastic part of demand.
options.why: Misconception: believing monopolists operate on the inelastic portion of demand; at Q=20 demand is elastic (MR>0) and profit-max is also in the elastic range.

options.text: Keep output at 20 thousand, because the $80 price exceeds the $20 marginal cost, so every unit already earns a profit.
options.why: Misconception: treating P > MC (positive per-unit profit) as a reason to stop; the decision rule compares MR, not price, with MC.

options.text: Decrease output, because lowering the price on all units makes marginal revenue less than the $80 price, so selling more reduces profit.
options.why: Misconception: correctly notes MR < P but wrongly concludes this means output should fall; the relevant comparison is MR (40) vs MC (20), and MR still exceeds MC.

options.text: Increase output to 50 thousand patches, because profit is maximized where price equals marginal cost.
options.why: Misconception: applying the perfect-competition P=MC rule to a monopolist; that is the efficient quantity, not the profit-maximizing one (Q=25).

options.text: Increase output, because marginal revenue of $40 exceeds marginal cost of $20, even though the price must fall on all units sold.
options.why: Correct: at Q=20, MR=120-80=40 > MC=20, so expanding adds more to revenue than to cost; profit-max is at MR=MC, Q=25, P=70.

s3-micro-32.explanation_en: A single-price monopolist maximizes profit where MR = MC. At 20 thousand patches, price is 120 - 2(20) = $80, but MR = 120 - 4(20) = $40, which is above MC of $20. Producing more adds more to revenue than to cost, so the firm should expand until MR = MC at 25 thousand patches (price $70). Keeping output unchanged because price exceeds MC is wrong, since the correct comparison is MR with MC. Cutting output because MR is below price is wrong, because MR is still above MC, so cutting loses profit.
