Producing 50 thousand where price equals MC applies the competitive rule and would give MR of -$80 on the last unit, below MC. Restricting output to raise price is wrong because the firm is in the elastic range where MR is positive and above MC, and profit-maximizing monopolists never produce in the inelastic range.

s3-micro-33.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm faces inverse demand P = 60 - 2Q and total cost TC = 100 + 10Q (so MC = 10). At its short-run profit-maximizing output, the firm earns a positive economic profit. Which of the following best explains how the long-run outcome for this firm occurs?

stimulus.description: Abstract cost and demand functions for one monopolistically competitive firm.

data.units: P in dollars per unit, Q in units per period
data.market_structure: monopolistic competition with free entry and exit; products are differentiated

options.text: Existing firms keep earning positive profit because product differentiation gives each firm a monopoly that entry cannot erode in the long run.
options.why: Misconception: believes product differentiation creates barriers to entry, so profit persists.

options.text: New firms enter with close substitutes, shifting this firm's demand left until price equals marginal cost, so the firm produces at the minimum of average total cost.
options.why: Misconception: confuses monopolistic competition with perfect competition, assuming P = MC and minimum-ATC production in the long run.

options.text: New firms enter with close substitutes, shifting this firm's demand left until price equals average total cost, so economic profit is zero while price still exceeds marginal cost.
options.why: Correct: positive profit attracts entry, each firm's demand shifts left and becomes more elastic until the demand curve is tangent to ATC (P = ATC, zero profit); the firm still sets MR = MC so P > MC.

options.text: New firms enter and shift this firm's demand right until marginal revenue equals average total cost, so economic profit is zero at a higher price.
options.why: Misconception: entry shifts demand right and the zero-profit condition involves MR = ATC; wrong direction and wrong condition.

options.text: Firms exit the market until the remaining firms' demand becomes perfectly elastic, so price equals marginal cost and profit is zero.
options.why: Misconception: positive profit causes exit and demand becomes perfectly elastic like perfect competition; exit occurs with losses, not profit.

s3-micro-33.explanation_en: At MR = MC: 60 - 4Q = 10 gives Q = 12.5, P = 35, ATC = 100/12.5 + 10 = 18, so profit is (35 - 18)(12.5) = 212.50 > 0. With free entry, positive profit attracts new firms selling close substitutes, which shifts each existing firm's demand left and makes it more elastic. This continues until demand is tangent to ATC, so P = ATC and economic profit is zero. The firm still produces where MR = MC, so price remains above marginal cost and output is below the minimum-ATC level. The option claiming price equals marginal cost at minimum ATC describes perfect competition and ignores the downward-sloping demand. The option claiming profit persists ignores that differentiation does not block entry. The option with a rightward shift gets the direction wrong, since entry reduces demand for each firm. The option with exit and perfectly elastic demand is wrong because exit happens with losses and demand stays downward sloping.

s3-micro-34.stem: In a laboratory experiment, two student-run firms simultaneously choose High or Low output once, with no communication, and the profits in the matrix shown are what each firm earns (Firm A, Firm B, in thousands of dollars). Which statement best interprets the outcome the experimenters should expect?

stimulus.description: Payoff matrix for two firms, Firm A (rows) and Firm B (columns), each choosing High output or Low output; payoffs in thousands of dollars of profit, listed as (A, B).

data.units: thousands of dollars of profit per period
data.play: simultaneous, one-shot, no communication or binding agreement

options.text: Both choose High output and each earns 30, because each firm expects the rival to choose Low output and wants to maximize its own gain.
options.why: Right outcome but wrong reasoning: High is best regardless of the rival's choice, not because the rival is expected to choose Low.

options.text: Both choose Low output and each earns 50, because that outcome gives the largest combined profit and is therefore stable.
options.why: Confuses the joint-profit-maximizing outcome with equilibrium; at Low, Low each firm gains by deviating to High (70>50).

options.text: Firm A chooses High output and earns 70 while Firm B chooses Low output and earns 10, because the firm moving first captures more profit.
options.why: Assumes sequential moves or a first-mover advantage, but the game is simultaneous and one-shot; Firm B would not choose Low since High is dominant.

options.text: Both choose High output and each earns 30, because High output yields the higher profit whatever the rival chooses, even though both would earn more at Low, Low.
options.why: Correct: High is dominant for both (70>50 and 30>10 for A; symmetric for B), so (High, High) with 30 each is the Nash equilibrium, worse than 50 each at Low, Low.

options.text: Firms randomly alternate between High and Low output, because no firm has a strategy that is best against every rival choice.
options.why: Claims no dominant strategy exists; in fact High is strictly dominant for both firms, so there is a pure-strategy equilibrium.

s3-micro-34.explanation_en: For Firm A, High output earns 30 versus 10 if B chooses High, and 70 versus 50 if B chooses Low, so High is always better. The matrix is symmetric, so the same is true for Firm B. Both choose High and earn 30 each, a Nash equilibrium. Both would be better off at Low, Low (50 each), but that outcome is not stable because each firm could raise its profit from 50 to 70 by deviating. The option claiming Low, Low is the equilibrium confuses joint-profit maximization with stability. The option about Firm A earning 70 while B earns 10 assumes a first-mover advantage that does not exist in a simultaneous one-shot game. The option reaching High, High by expecting the rival to choose Low gives the wrong reason, since the choice does not depend on the rival's move. The option about random alternation is wrong because both firms have a dominant strategy.

s3-micro-35.stem: Two firms play the one-shot, simultaneous game shown, with payoffs (Firm X, Firm Y) in dollars of profit: both choose A gives (6, 6); X chooses A and Y chooses B gives (2, 8); X chooses B and Y chooses A gives (8, 2); both choose B gives (4, 4). Which of the following is the best interpretation of the outcome of this game?

stimulus.description: Two-player simultaneous game. Rows: Player X chooses A or B. Columns: Player Y chooses A or B. Cell entries are (X payoff, Y payoff) in dollars of profit.

options.text: Both firms choose B and each earns 4, which is the highest payoff either firm can guarantee, so neither would gain by choosing A even if the other chose A.
options.why: Misconception: treating the equilibrium as a gain-maximizing choice and claiming no gain from choosing A if the other chose A; this is false, since if Y chose A, X would gain by choosing B (8 vs 6).

options.text: Both firms choose A and each earns 6, because that outcome gives the highest combined profit.
options.why: Misconception: assuming firms reach the joint-profit-maximizing outcome without a binding agreement; ignores each firm's incentive to deviate to B.

options.text: Firm X chooses B and earns 8, while Firm Y chooses A and earns 2, because X moves to its best payoff first.
options.why: Misconception: assuming a simultaneous game has a first mover and that one firm can exploit the other; Y would never choose A since B is dominant.

options.text: Both firms choose B and each earns 4, which is 2 less than each would earn if both chose A, because B is each firm's dominant strategy.
options.why: Correct: B gives X 8 vs 6 if Y plays A and 4 vs 2 if Y plays B, and the same holds for Y. So (B,B) is the Nash equilibrium with 4 each, 2 less than the 6 each at (A,A).

options.text: There is no stable outcome, because each firm's best choice changes depending on what the other firm chooses.
options.why: Misconception: believing a best response that depends on the rival means no equilibrium; here each firm has a dominant strategy, so the best choice does not change.

s3-micro-35.explanation_en: For Firm X, B pays 8 rather than 6 if Y chooses A, and 4 rather than 2 if Y chooses B, so B is dominant. Firm Y's payoffs are symmetric, so B is also dominant for Y. The Nash equilibrium is both choosing B with 4 each. Both choosing A would give 6 each, so the equilibrium leaves each firm 2 worse off, which is the prisoners' dilemma pattern. The both-choose-A option is wrong because it is not stable, since each firm gains by deviating. The option with X earning 8 and Y earning 2 is wrong because Y would not choose its dominated strategy and the game is simultaneous. The option claiming that neither firm would gain by choosing A even if the other chose A is wrong because X would earn 8 rather than 6 by deviating to B against A. The no-stable-outcome option is wrong because each firm has a dominant strategy, so the equilibrium is stable.

s3-micro-36.stem: A small bakery sells bread at $3 per loaf and can hire as many workers as it wants at a wage of $14 per hour. The table shows each additional worker's marginal product. Which of the following describes how the bakery's demand for labor as a factor of production is determined, and how many workers it hires to maximize profit?

stimulus.description: Table of marginal product of labor for a bakery by worker number, with bread price and wage.

columns: Marginal product of labor (loaves per hour)
data.notes: Bakery is a price taker in the bread market and the labor market; workers are hired one at a time.

options.text: Labor demand is independent of the demand for bread; the bakery hires 1 worker because the first worker has the highest marginal product.
options.why: Misconception: believes the firm stops at the highest marginal product rather than hiring until MRP equals the wage, and denies derived demand.

options.text: Labor demand is derived from the demand for bread; the bakery hires 4 workers because the price of a loaf exceeds the wage for every worker hired.
options.why: Misconception: compares the output price with the wage instead of marginal revenue product, ignoring diminishing marginal product.

options.text: Labor demand is derived from the demand for bread; the bakery hires 2 workers because the third worker's marginal product of 5 loaves is below the wage of $14.
options.why: Misconception: compares marginal product in loaves directly with a wage in dollars, forgetting to multiply by the price to get MRP.

options.text: Labor demand is independent of the demand for bread; the bakery hires 5 workers because every worker adds some output to production.
options.why: Misconception: thinks any positive marginal product justifies hiring and denies that factor demand is derived from product demand.

options.text: Labor demand is derived from the demand for bread; the bakery hires 3 workers because the third worker's marginal revenue product exceeds the wage but the fourth worker's does not.
options.why: Correct: derived demand; MRP = MP x P gives 27, 21, 15, 12, 6, so workers 1-3 have MRP above $14 and worker 4 (12) does not.

s3-micro-36.explanation_en: Firms demand factors such as labor because of the output they help produce, so factor demand is derived from product demand. The profit-maximizing firm hires workers as long as marginal revenue product (MP x price) is at least the wage. MRP is 27, 21, 15, 12 and 6 for workers 1 to 5. Workers 1 through 3 each have an MRP above $14, while worker 4 has an MRP of $12, below the wage, so the bakery hires 3. Comparing the loaf price with the wage ignores diminishing marginal product and would wrongly hire a fourth worker. Comparing marginal product in loaves with a dollar wage skips the multiplication by price and wrongly stops at 2. Hiring everyone with positive output ignores cost. Stopping at the highest marginal product ignores that additional workers still add more revenue than they cost. Labor demand is not independent of product demand.

s3-micro-37.stem: A firm sells its output in a perfectly competitive market at 3 dollars per unit and hires factor X in a perfectly competitive factor market. Its marginal product of X is given in the table. Which of the following correctly describes the firm's demand for factor X?

stimulus.description: Table of a firm's marginal product (MP) of an abstract factor X at each quantity of X, with the output price initially 3 dollars per unit.

columns: Marginal product of X (units of output)

options.text: It is upward sloping, because each additional unit of X adds more to total revenue than the one before it.
options.why: Ignores diminishing marginal returns; the table shows MP falling, so MRP and factor demand slope downward.

options.text: It is derived from the demand for the output, so if the wage of X rises, the demand curve for X shifts to the left.
options.why: Confuses a change in the factor's own price (wage) with a determinant of demand; a wage change causes movement along the demand curve, not a shift.

options.text: It is independent of the output market, so a rise in the output price from 3 to 4 dollars moves the firm along its demand curve for X.
options.why: Denies derived demand; treats factor demand as independent of the product market and confuses a shift with a movement along the curve.

options.text: It is the marginal product curve measured in units of output, so a rise in the output price from 3 to 4 dollars leaves it unchanged.
options.why: Confuses marginal product (physical units) with marginal revenue product (dollars); ignores that output price scales the demand curve.

options.text: It is derived from the demand for the output, so if the output price rises from 3 to 4 dollars, the demand curve for X shifts to the right.
options.why: Correct: factor demand is derived demand, MRP = P x MP; a higher output price raises MRP at every quantity, shifting demand right (e.g., MRP of the 3rd unit rises from 18 to 24).

s3-micro-37.explanation_en: In a perfectly competitive output market, the firm's demand for a factor is its marginal revenue product, MRP = P x MP. With P = 3, MRP for units 1 to 5 is 30, 24, 18, 12, 6; with P = 4 it is 40, 32, 24, 16, 8, higher at every quantity, so the demand for X shifts right. This is what it means for factor demand to be derived from output demand. The option saying a wage increase shifts demand left is wrong because the wage is the factor's own price, so a wage change moves the firm along the demand curve. The option claiming independence from the output market is wrong because the output price directly determines MRP. The option saying demand is unchanged confuses physical marginal product with marginal revenue product measured in dollars. The upward-sloping option is wrong because MP falls as more X is used (10, 8, 6, 4, 2), so MRP slopes downward.

s3-micro-38.stem: A strawberry farm sells flats at a constant price of $4 in a perfectly competitive market and hires pickers at a market wage of $65 per day. Using the table, how many workers will the profit-maximizing farm hire?

stimulus.description: Table of number of workers and total flats of strawberries picked per day on a farm.

data.title: Daily strawberry harvest
data.notes: Strawberries sell in a perfectly competitive output market; pickers are hired in a perfectly competitive labor market.

options.text: 4 workers
options.why: Correct: the 4th worker's MRP is $72, which is at least $65, and the 5th worker's MRP is $60, which is below $65.

options.text: 3 workers
options.why: Stops too early; the fourth worker's MRP of $72 still exceeds the $65 wage, so hiring adds profit.

options.text: 1 worker
options.why: Picks the worker with the highest marginal product, ignoring that MRP still exceeds the wage for later workers.

options.text: 5 workers
options.why: Assumes hiring continues to the point where MRP is nearest the wage, or at $60 mistakenly treated as the wage; the 5th worker adds $60 of revenue but costs $65.

options.text: 7 workers
options.why: Maximizes output by hiring until marginal product is lowest, ignoring cost; MRP of $36 is far below the wage.

s3-micro-38.explanation_en: A competitive firm hires labor until marginal revenue product (price times marginal product) falls to the wage. Marginal products are 30, 25, 22, 18, 15, 12, 9, so MRP is 120, 100, 88, 72, 60, 48, 36. The fourth worker adds $72 of revenue for a $65 wage, so hiring that worker raises profit. The fifth adds only $60 for $65, so hiring that worker lowers profit. The farm hires 4 workers. Hiring only 1 or 3 forgoes workers whose MRP exceeds the wage. Hiring 5 adds a worker whose MRP is below the wage. Hiring 7 maximizes output rather than profit and ignores the wage.

s3-micro-39.stem: A bakery is a price taker in both the bread market and the labor market. It sells each loaf for $2 and pays each worker $30 per day. The table shows its total output at each level of daily labor. To maximize profit, how many workers should the bakery hire, and why?

stimulus.description: Table of daily labor, total loaves, for a bakery that sells loaves at $2 each and pays $30 per worker per day.

data.market_structure: Bakery is a price taker in both the loaf market and the labor market

options.text: 4 workers, because the fourth worker adds $40 in revenue for a $30 wage, while a fifth would add only $28
options.why: Correct: hire while MRP (P x MP) is at least the wage; worker 4 has MRP 40 > 30, worker 5 has MRP 28 < 30.

options.text: 2 workers, because the second worker has the highest marginal product, 40 loaves
options.why: Confuses maximum marginal product with the profit-maximizing hiring level; ignores wage and price.

options.text: 3 workers, because the third worker's $60 of added revenue exceeds the $30 wage by the widest gap that is still above the wage
options.why: Stops at a point where the gap is still large rather than hiring until MRP falls to the wage; ignores that worker 4 still adds profit.

options.text: 5 workers, because the fifth worker's 14 extra loaves still yield positive output and nearly cover the wage
options.why: Hires a worker whose MRP ($28) is below the wage ($30), which lowers profit; treats positive output as sufficient.

options.text: 6 workers, because total output keeps rising with each added worker
options.why: Believes maximizing output maximizes profit; ignores marginal cost of labor.

s3-micro-39.explanation_en: Because the bakery is a price taker, marginal revenue product of labor is $2 times marginal product. Marginal products are 30, 40, 30, 20, 14, 10, so MRP is $60, $80, $60, $40, $28, $20. The wage is a constant $30. Hiring the fourth worker adds $40 of revenue for $30 of cost, which raises profit by $10. The fifth worker adds only $28 for $30, lowering profit by $2, so the bakery stops at 4 workers. Hiring only 2 workers uses the point of highest marginal product, which is irrelevant to the wage comparison. Stopping at 3 workers forgoes the fourth worker's $10 gain, since the goal is to hire until MRP falls to the wage, not to maximize the gap. Hiring 5 workers adds a worker whose MRP is below the wage. Hiring 6 workers wrongly treats output maximization as the goal and ignores labor cost.

s3-micro-40.stem: A firm is a price taker in both its product market and its labor market. It sells each unit of output for $4 and pays each worker $18. Workers are hired one at a time, and total product is shown in the table. To maximize profit, how many workers should the firm hire?

stimulus.description: Total product of labor for a firm selling output at $4 per unit and hiring labor at $18 per worker.

data.market_structure: perfectly competitive in both product and labor markets

options.text: 1 worker
options.why: Stops too early: the student thinks the first worker is best because it has the highest marginal product, ignoring that the second worker's MRP of $20 still exceeds the $18 wage.

options.text: 2 workers
options.why: Correct: MRP of the 1st worker is $24 and of the 2nd is $20, both at least $18, while the 3rd worker's MRP is $16, below the wage.

options.text: 3 workers
options.why: Hires one worker too many: the student includes the first worker whose MRP ($16) is below the wage, or compares average revenue product ($20) with the wage.

options.text: 4 workers
options.why: Compares average revenue product with the wage: 4 x 18/4 = $18 equals the wage, so the student hires 4, ignoring that marginal, not average, revenue product governs hiring.

options.text: 7 workers
options.why: Hires until marginal product is smallest or until output stops rising, ignoring the wage entirely.

s3-micro-40.explanation_en: In a perfectly competitive factor market the firm hires labor as long as the marginal revenue product (price times marginal physical product) is at least the wage. Marginal products are 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.5 and 1, so MRP is $24, $20, $16, $12, $8, $6 and $4. The 1st and 2nd workers add at least $18 to revenue, but the 3rd adds only $16, so the firm hires 2 workers. Hiring only 1 worker gives up the second worker's $2 net gain. Hiring 3 adds a worker whose MRP is below the wage and so lowers profit. Hiring 4 relies on average revenue product, which equals $18 there, but the hiring rule uses marginal, not average, values. Hiring 7 ignores the wage altogether.

s3-micro-41.stem: The graph shows the labor market for a research station that is the only employer of field technicians in its region. Which statement best explains why the station hires 24 technicians at $20 per hour?

stimulus.description: Labor market for seasonal field technicians at a single agricultural research station, showing labor supply, marginal factor cost, and marginal revenue product curves.

y_axis.label: Hourly wage / marginal cost / marginal revenue product

curves.label: Marginal revenue product (MRP = demand for labor)

labeled_points.label: Wage on supply curve at L=24
Competitive intersection of S and MRP

data.note: The research station is the only employer of technicians in the region.

options.text: At 24 technicians, MRP equals the $20 wage, so the station hires until the last worker's product value equals what that worker is paid.
options.why: Misconception: applying the competitive rule MRP = wage; at L=24 MRP is $32, not $20.

options.text: At 24 technicians, MRP equals MFC at $32, and the station pays only the $20 wage needed on the supply curve to attract 24 workers.
options.why: Correct: hires where MRP = MFC (24, $32), then reads the wage from the supply curve ($20).

options.text: At 24 technicians, the labor supply curve intersects MRP at $32, so the station pays workers their full marginal revenue product.
options.why: Misconception: believing supply meets MRP at the monopsony quantity; supply is $20 there, and the S-MRP intersection is at L=36, $26.

options.text: At 24 technicians, MFC equals the $20 wage, so the station stops hiring because adding a worker would not raise its total labor cost.
options.why: Misconception: confusing MFC with the wage; MFC at 24 is $32 and exceeds the wage because the higher wage applies to all workers.

options.text: At 24 technicians, the station has hired fewer workers than the competitive level because it must raise the wage by $32 to attract one more worker.
options.why: Misconception: misreading MFC as the wage increase needed; $32 is the marginal cost of the 24th worker, not a wage raise, and it does not explain the stopping rule.

s3-micro-41.explanation_en: A profit-maximizing monopsonist hires until MRP equals MFC. Here 44 - 0.5L = 8 + L gives L = 24 and MRP = MFC = $32. The wage is read from the supply curve at 24 workers: 8 + 0.5(24) = $20. MFC lies above supply because hiring one more worker requires raising the wage for all workers. The option claiming MRP equals the wage is wrong because MRP is $32 at 24 workers, not $20. The option claiming supply meets MRP at 24 is wrong because that intersection is at 36 workers and $26, which is the competitive outcome. The option claiming MFC equals the wage is wrong because MFC is $32, above the $20 wage. The option about a $32 wage raise is wrong because $32 is the marginal cost of the last worker, not a wage increase, and it does not state the MRP = MFC rule.

s3-micro-42.stem: In the labor market described by the equations above, the firm maximizes profit. Which of the following best explains why the firm hires 12 workers at a wage of $8 per hour rather than 18 workers at $11 per hour?

stimulus.description: Abstract labor market with a single buyer of labor, given by linear equations.

data.units: W and MRP in dollars per hour; L in number of workers
data.market_structure: One firm is the only employer (monopsony) and must pay all workers the same wage; the firm sells its output in a perfectly competitive market.

options.text: The firm hires where the labor supply curve intersects the marginal revenue product curve, which occurs at 12 workers.
options.why: Misconception: using the competitive-market equilibrium rule; that intersection is at 18 workers and $11.

options.text: The wage equals the marginal revenue product at 12 workers, so the firm has no incentive to hire more workers.
options.why: Misconception: applying the competitive rule W = MRP. At 12 workers MRP = 14, not 8.

options.text: The marginal revenue product of labor is below the wage at 12 workers, so hiring fewer workers raises profit.
options.why: Misconception: misreading the numbers; at 12 workers MRP = 14, which is above the wage of 8, so the claim is false.

options.text: Hiring each additional worker requires raising the wage for all workers, so the marginal factor cost of labor exceeds the wage and equals MRP at 12 workers.
options.why: Correct: MFC = 2 + L lies above the supply wage; MRP = MFC at L = 12 gives W = 2 + 6 = 8.

options.text: Because the firm is the only employer, the wage it pays equals the marginal factor cost of labor at each quantity of workers.
options.why: Misconception: treating a monopsonist as a wage taker whose MFC equals the wage; with an upward-sloping supply curve, MFC lies above the wage.

s3-micro-42.explanation_en: The monopsonist faces the upward-sloping market labor supply curve, so to hire one more worker it must raise the wage paid to all workers. Its marginal factor cost is therefore MFC = 2 + L, which lies above the supply wage. Profit is maximized where MRP = MFC: 20 - 0.5L = 2 + L gives L = 12. The wage is read from the supply curve: W = 2 + 0.5(12) = $8. The option claiming wage equals MRP at 12 workers is wrong because MRP there is $14, and that rule describes competitive hiring, which would give 18 workers at $11. The option saying MRP is below the wage is wrong because $14 exceeds $8. The option using the supply and MRP intersection is wrong because that intersection is at 18 workers, not 12. The option claiming the wage equals MFC is wrong because MFC exceeds the wage when supply slopes upward.

s3-micro-43.stem: The graph shows the market for hive rentals. The market equilibrium quantity is 20 hives. Which of the following correctly describes the market outcome relative to the socially efficient outcome?

stimulus.description: Market for orchard-hive rentals. Downward-sloping private demand (marginal private benefit), a higher parallel marginal social benefit curve, and an upward-sloping supply curve (marginal cost, equal to marginal social cost).

x_axis.label: Quantity of hive rentals per season

data.note: Each hive rented also pollinates neighboring orchards that do not pay, a benefit of $20 per hive.

options.text: The market produces too few hives, because marginal social benefit exceeds marginal cost at 20 hives.
options.why: Correct: at Q=20, MSB=80 > MC=60, so expanding to Q=25 raises total surplus; the market underproduces.

options.text: The market produces too many hives, because marginal social benefit exceeds marginal cost at 20 hives.
options.why: Misconception: confuses the direction of the inefficiency; if MSB > MC, output is too low, not too high.

options.text: The market produces too few hives, because marginal private benefit exceeds marginal cost at 20 hives.
options.why: Right direction but wrong reasoning: at 20 hives MPB equals MC (both 60), so MPB does not exceed MC; the gap involves MSB.

options.text: The market produces the efficient quantity, because marginal private benefit equals marginal cost at 20 hives.
options.why: Misconception: assumes private equilibrium is automatically efficient and ignores the external benefit.

options.text: The market produces too many hives, because marginal cost exceeds marginal private benefit at 20 hives.
options.why: Misconception: treats the positive externality as a cost problem; at 20 hives MC equals MPB, not exceeds it.

s3-micro-43.explanation_en: Market equilibrium is where MPB equals MC: 100-2Q = 20+2Q gives Q=20 and P=60. The socially efficient quantity is where MSB equals MC: 120-2Q = 20+2Q gives Q=25. At 20 hives, MSB is 80 while MC is 60, so one more hive adds more social benefit than cost, and the market produces too few hives. The too-many options reverse the direction of the inefficiency. The option claiming marginal private benefit exceeds marginal cost is false, since they are equal at 20. The option claiming efficiency ignores the $20 external benefit that private demand leaves out. The option claiming marginal cost exceeds marginal private benefit is false at the equilibrium, where the two are equal.

s3-micro-44.stem: Based on the table, which of the following correctly describes a market outcome in which 25 units are produced?

stimulus.description: Table of marginal benefit and marginal cost at selected quantities for a good with no externalities.

data.note: Marginal benefit (demand) is P = 100 - 2Q; marginal cost (supply) is P = 20 + 2Q; both linear between listed points. No externalities.

options.text: It is efficient because producing more units always increases total surplus as long as marginal benefit remains positive.
options.why: Misconception: believes efficiency means maximizing quantity while MB is positive, ignoring marginal cost.

options.text: It is inefficient because underproduction occurs; the units from 20 to 25 are worth more to buyers than they cost to produce, creating a deadweight loss of $50.
options.why: Misconception: confuses direction of inefficiency; at 25 units MC > MB, so this is overproduction, not underproduction.

options.text: It is inefficient because overproduction occurs; the units from 20 to 25 cost more to produce than they are worth to buyers, creating a deadweight loss of $50.
options.why: Correct: MC exceeds MB for units 21-25, so these units reduce total surplus; the loss triangle is 0.5*5*20 = $50.

options.text: It is efficient because the 25th unit is sold at a price that still exceeds the marginal cost of the first unit produced.
options.why: Misconception: compares price to the cost of the first unit rather than comparing MB and MC at the margin.

options.text: It is inefficient because overproduction occurs, creating a deadweight loss of $100, the full triangle between the curves from 20 to 25 units.
options.why: Misconception: correct direction but computes the triangle area without the one-half factor (5*20 = 100).

s3-micro-44.explanation_en: The efficient quantity is where marginal benefit equals marginal cost: 100 - 2Q = 20 + 2Q gives Q = 20 (both $60). At 25 units, MB is $50 and MC is $70, so the extra units cost more than they are worth to buyers; this is overproduction. The gap grows from $0 at 20 units to $20 at 25 units, so the deadweight loss is 0.5 x 5 x 20 = $50. The underproduction option reverses the direction of the gap. The option claiming more output is always better ignores marginal cost. The option comparing price with the first unit's cost does not use the marginal comparison at the 25th unit. The $100 option omits the one-half in the triangle area.

s3-micro-45.stem: Based on the graph, which of the following correctly describes the unregulated market outcome compared with the socially efficient outcome?

stimulus.description: Market for a flu vaccine showing marginal private benefit (demand), marginal social benefit, and marginal cost (supply) as straight lines.

data.note: Each vaccination gives other people a benefit of $20 (reduced spread of disease). There are no external costs.

options.text: The market produces 20,000 vaccinations, which is socially efficient, because marginal private benefit equals marginal cost at that quantity.
options.why: Misconception: equates the market equilibrium with social efficiency, ignoring the external benefit in MSB.

options.text: The market produces 20,000 vaccinations, which is more than the socially efficient 25,000, because marginal private benefit exceeds marginal cost at 20,000.
options.why: Misconception: confuses direction of inefficiency (positive externality leads to overproduction) and misreads MPB > MC as a reason for excess output; at Q = 20 MPB equals MC.

options.text: The market produces 20,000 vaccinations, which is less than the socially efficient 25,000, because marginal social benefit exceeds marginal cost at 20,000.
options.why: Correct: the market sets MPB = MC at Q = 20; at that quantity MSB = 80 exceeds MC = 60, so output is below the efficient 25 where MSB = MC.

options.text: The market produces 25,000 vaccinations, which is socially efficient, because marginal social benefit equals marginal cost at that quantity.
options.why: Misconception: thinks the market itself reaches the social optimum; the unregulated market ignores the external benefit and stops at 20.

options.text: The market produces 20,000 vaccinations, which is less than the socially efficient 25,000, because the price of $60 is below the socially efficient price of $70.
options.why: Right quantities but wrong reasoning: inefficiency is defined by MSB exceeding MC at the market quantity, not by a price difference.

s3-micro-45.explanation_en: Without intervention, buyers and sellers consider only private benefit and cost, so the market clears where demand (MPB) equals supply (MC): 100 - 2Q = 20 + 2Q gives Q = 20 thousand and P = $60. The socially efficient quantity is where MSB equals MC: 120 - 2Q = 20 + 2Q gives Q = 25 thousand. At 20 thousand, MSB is $80 while MC is $60, so the marginal vaccination is worth more to society than it costs, and the market underproduces. The option claiming overproduction is wrong because the external benefit is positive, so output is too low, not too high. The option calling 20 thousand efficient is wrong because MPB = MC ignores the $20 external benefit. The option saying the market produces 25 thousand is wrong because the market stops at 20 thousand. The option citing the price gap is wrong because the inefficiency is defined by MSB exceeding MC at the market quantity (a quantity-based comparison), not by the market price being lower than another price.

s3-micro-46.stem: Researchers at the field station want to fund a service that, once provided, can be used by everyone in the bay at no additional cost to the provider and cannot be withheld from anyone who refuses to pay. According to the table, which service is an example of a pure public good, and which problem is most likely to arise if it is funded only by voluntary payments?

stimulus.description: Table of four services offered at a coastal research field station, with whether one more user reduces others' use (rivalry) and whether non-payers can be kept from using it (excludability).

data.title: Services at Tern Point Field Station
columns: Does one user's use reduce what is available to others?
Can non-payers be prevented from using it?
rows: Open-access tide-warning siren heard across the whole bay
Fishing in the unregulated bay (no permit required)
Members-only data portal with unlimited simultaneous logins

options.text: The members-only data portal; free riding leads to underprovision
options.why: Misclassifies a club good (nonrival but excludable) as a public good; nonpayers can be kept out, so free riding is not the key problem.

options.text: The tide-warning siren; overuse leads to depletion of the resource
options.why: Confuses public goods with common resources: correctly picks the siren but names depletion from overuse, which does not occur for a nonrival good.

options.text: Fishing in the unregulated bay; free riding leads to underprovision
options.why: Misclassifies a common resource (rival, nonexcludable) as a public good because it is nonexcludable, ignoring rivalry.

options.text: The tide-warning siren; free riding leads to underprovision
options.why: Correct: the siren is nonrival and nonexcludable, a pure public good, and because people can benefit without paying, voluntary funding leads to free riding and underprovision.

options.text: Fee-only sample freezer space; overuse leads to depletion of the resource
options.why: Misclassifies a private good (rival and excludable) as having an overuse problem; fees prevent depletion and it is not a public good.

s3-micro-46.explanation_en: The siren is nonrival (one person hearing it does not reduce others' benefit) and nonexcludable (no one can be kept from hearing it), so it is a pure public good. Because nonpayers still benefit, individuals have an incentive to free ride, so voluntary payment leads to underprovision. Unregulated fishing is rival but nonexcludable, which makes it a common resource, not a public good. The members-only portal is nonrival but excludable, a club good, so nonpayers can be blocked and free riding is not the central issue. Freezer space is rival and excludable, a private good, and the overuse-depletion problem does not apply to a nonrival siren.

s3-micro-47.stem: Using the table, which good is a pure public good?

stimulus.description: Table of five abstract goods labeled V, W, X, Y, Z with whether non-payers can be excluded and whether one person's use reduces the amount available to others.

columns: Can non-payers be excluded from using it?
Does one person's use reduce the amount available to others?
rows: Yes, but only after usage exceeds a capacity limit

options.text: Good V, because non-payers can be excluded and use is rival
options.why: Describes a private good (excludable and rival); student confuses private with public.

options.text: Good W, because non-payers can be excluded and use is nonrival
options.why: Describes a club/natural-monopoly-type good (excludable, nonrival); student thinks nonrival alone makes a good public.

options.text: Good X, because non-payers cannot be excluded and use is rival
options.why: Describes a common resource (nonexcludable, rival); student thinks nonexcludability alone makes a good public.

options.text: Good Y, because non-payers cannot be excluded and use is nonrival
options.why: Key: nonexcludable and nonrival are both required for a pure public good.

options.text: Good Z, because non-payers can be excluded and rivalry arises only past capacity
options.why: Excludable good with congestion; student treats partial rivalry as public, but exclusion is possible so it is not pure public.

s3-micro-47.explanation_en: A pure public good is both nonexcludable and nonrival. The good that non-payers cannot be kept from using and whose use does not reduce availability to others fits exactly. The excludable and rival good is a private good. The excludable and nonrival good is a club-type good, since exclusion is possible. The nonexcludable and rival good is a common resource, since use by one reduces what remains for others. The excludable good with capacity-limited rivalry can be priced, so it is not a pure public good.

s3-micro-48.stem: The table shows the percent of total income received by each quintile of households in Maple County before and after a tax-and-transfer program. Based on the table, which of the following is the outcome of the program?

stimulus.description: Table of household income shares by quintile in Maple County before and after a tax-and-transfer program.

data.title: Share of total county income received by each quintile of households (percent)

options.text: The Lorenz curve shifts away from the line of equality because the lowest 20% of households' share rises by only 3 percentage points.
options.why: Misconception: judges inequality by the size of the gain rather than its direction; any rise in the poorest share with a fall in the richest share reduces inequality.

options.text: The Lorenz curve shifts away from the line of equality because the highest 20% of households still receive the largest share of income.
options.why: Misconception: confuses inequality remaining with inequality increasing; the top share fell from 51% to 43%, so inequality decreased even though the top quintile still has the most.

options.text: The Lorenz curve shifts toward the line of equality because the lowest 60% of households' cumulative income share rises from 27% to 37%.
options.why: Correct direction but arithmetic error: 7+12+16 is 35, not 37, so the stated cumulative share is wrong.

options.text: The Lorenz curve is unchanged because the fourth quintile's income share stays at 22% and total income is still 100%.
options.why: Misconception: thinks one unchanged quintile or an unchanged total means no change in distribution; the Lorenz curve uses cumulative shares, which did change.

options.text: The Lorenz curve shifts toward the line of equality because the lowest 60% of households' cumulative income share rises from 27% to 35%.
options.why: Correct: cumulative bottom-60% share is 4+9+14=27 before and 7+12+16=35 after, so the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality and the Gini coefficient falls.

s3-micro-48.explanation_en: Cumulative shares for the lowest 60% of households are 4+9+14 = 27% before and 7+12+16 = 35% after. Lowest-40% cumulative shares also rise (13% to 19%) while the top quintile falls from 51% to 43%. Every point on the Lorenz curve is therefore closer to the line of equality, so inequality falls, and the option stating 35% is correct. The option saying the curve moves away is wrong because the top quintile still receiving the largest share does not mean inequality rose; it fell. The option stating 37% has an arithmetic error, since the cumulative share is 35%. The option claiming no change is wrong because the unchanged fourth quintile and the 100% total do not offset the changes in the other quintiles, and the cumulative shares changed. The option citing only a 3-point gain for the lowest 20% is wrong because the poorest share rising while the richest share falls moves the curve toward equality regardless of the size of the gain.

s3-micro-49.stem: Using the table, which of the following correctly describes the effect of the policy on the distribution of income?

stimulus.description: Incomes of five equal-sized groups before and after a tax-and-transfer policy, in thousands of dollars per group.

data.note: Each group contains 20 percent of the population. Policy: $20 thousand is taxed from Group 5; $10 thousand is transferred to each of Groups 1 and 2.

options.text: The highest 20 percent of the population's income share falls from 50 percent to 40 percent, and the Gini coefficient rises.
options.why: The top share is actually 100/200=50% before and 80/200=40% after, but the claim that Gini rises is wrong; a falling top share and rising bottom shares reduce the Gini.

options.text: The lowest 40 percent of the population's income share rises from 15 percent to 25 percent, and the Lorenz curve moves farther from the line of equality.
options.why: Computes the share correctly but reverses the Lorenz curve interpretation: a higher cumulative share at a given population point means closer to equality, not farther.

options.text: The lowest 40 percent of the population's income share rises from 15 percent to 20 percent, and the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality.
options.why: Miscalculates the new share (e.g., 40/200) by omitting part of the transfer, though the direction is right.

options.text: The lowest 40 percent of the population's income share stays at 15 percent because total income is unchanged, and the Lorenz curve does not move.
options.why: Confuses unchanged total income with unchanged distribution; a transfer changes shares even when the total is fixed.

options.text: The lowest 40 percent of the population's income share rises from 15 percent to 25 percent, and the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality.
options.why: Correct: bottom-two cumulative share goes from 30/200=15% to 50/200=25%; every cumulative share rises, so the Lorenz curve moves toward equality.

s3-micro-49.explanation_en: Total income stays at 200. Before the policy, the lowest 40 percent hold (10+20)/200 = 15 percent. After, they hold (20+30)/200 = 25 percent. Cumulative shares for the lowest 20, 40, 60 and 80 percent rise from 5, 15, 30 and 50 percent to 10, 25, 40 and 60 percent, so the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality and inequality falls. The option with the curve moving farther from equality reverses this interpretation. The option with a 20 percent share miscalculates the new share. The option with an unchanged share ignores that a transfer changes the distribution even when total income is fixed. The option with a rising Gini is wrong because the top share falls from 50 to 40 percent while lower shares rise, which lowers the Gini coefficient.

s3-micro-50.stem: A players' association adopts a policy that moves $5 million per year from the highest quintile to the lowest quintile. Total earnings and the earnings of the other three quintiles do not change. Compared with the situation before the policy, which of the following is the outcome?

stimulus.description: Table of annual prize earnings by income quintile for 500 professional esports players, in millions of dollars, before any policy.

data.title: Annual prize earnings of professional esports players by quintile (100 players per quintile)

options.text: The lowest 40% of players receive 19% of total earnings, and the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality.
options.why: Key: after the transfer the lowest quintile has 9 and the second has 10, so the bottom 40% hold 19 of 100 = 19%. A transfer from rich to poor raises the lower cumulative shares, so the Lorenz curve moves toward the line of equality.

options.text: The lowest 40% of players receive 19% of total earnings, and the Lorenz curve moves farther from the line of equality.
options.why: Gets the 19% share right but reverses the direction: the student thinks that raising the bottom share bows the Lorenz curve away from equality (confuses Lorenz curve position with the Gini direction).

options.text: The lowest 40% of players receive 14% of total earnings, and the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality.
options.why: Uses the pre-policy bottom-40% share (4+10=14%), ignoring the transfer, while correctly stating the direction of the change.

options.text: The lowest 40% of players receive 9% of total earnings, and the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality.
options.why: Reports only the new lowest-quintile share (9%) instead of the cumulative share of the lowest two quintiles.

options.text: The lowest 40% of players receive 24% of total earnings, and the Lorenz curve moves farther from the line of equality.
options.why: Adds the $5 million transfer to both of the bottom two quintiles (14+10=24), double-counting the transfer, and also gets the direction wrong.

s3-micro-50.explanation_en: Before the policy, the lowest two quintiles earn 4 + 10 = 14 of 100, or 14%. After moving $5 million from the top to the bottom quintile, the lowest quintile earns 9 and the second earns 10, so the bottom 40% earn 19 of 100 = 19%. Because the cumulative share of the bottom groups rises (and the top falls), the Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality, meaning less inequality. The option showing 19% with a curve farther from equality has the direction backwards. The 14% option ignores the transfer. The 9% option reports only the lowest quintile rather than the cumulative share of the lowest 40%. The 24% option double-counts the transfer, and its direction is also wrong.
